# Lion

> Lion is a JSON-based Lisp with a built-in Datalog logic database, an exact symbolic solver and proof kernel, and an Effect v4 runtime. Every Lion program is valid JSON — storable in a database, diffable in Git, verifiable statically with `lion check`, and evaluable in memory or in a browser Web Worker.

Full reference in one file: https://lionlang.dev/llms-full.txt
Interactive documentation: https://lionlang.dev/docs.html
Changelog: https://lionlang.dev/changelog.html
Repository: https://github.com/andrueandersoncs/lion

## Core Syntax Rules (Read First)

- Every program is valid JSON. No separate parser.
- Arrays are calls: `["number/add", 1, 2]` -> `3`. Empty array `[]` evaluates to itself.
- Literal lists must use `["quote", [1, 2]]` or `["array/make", 1, 2]`.
- Strings resolve to bindings declared in an enclosing scope (stdlib, environment, `define`, `relation`, `schema`, lambda params); undeclared strings evaluate to themselves, EXCEPT:
  - `"?name"` is a logic variable (`"?_"` is anonymous).
  - A misspelled `"module/name"` (e.g. `"number/ad"`) is an error. Use `["quote", "name"]` when you mean a literal string that collides with a binding or variable.
- Objects preserve their keys and evaluate each value.
- Numbers use exact rational/decimal arithmetic (no floating-point rounding drift).
- Always run `lion check` on generated programs before executing them to catch arity errors, typos, unreachable `match` branches, and unsafe rules with JSON-pointer locations.

## Packages

- `@lionlang/core` (v0.18.0): Evaluator, special forms, standard library, Datalog logic engine, schemas, symbolic solver (`proof/prove`, `proof/bounds`, `proof/rules`, `proof/sensitivity`, `proof/valid?`), and graph algorithms (`graph/`).
- `@lionlang/ui` (v0.1.0): Declarative, interactive, and streaming UI bindings (`ui/stack`, `ui/card`, `ui/metric`, `ui/alert`, `ui/table`, `ui/slider`, `ui/input`, `ui/select`, `ui/toggle`, `ui/button`, `ui/why`, `ui/proof`) plus a zero-dependency DOM renderer (`@lionlang/ui/dom`) and stateful `createUiSession()`.
- `@lionlang/cli` (v0.17.0): The `lion` CLI — evaluate files/stdin/`-e`, persist logic databases (`--database`), static check & lint (`lion check`), inspect/diff databases (`lion inspect`, `lion diff --derived`), serve the Fold Map visual graph editor (`lion repl`), and emit a browser Web Worker (`lion worker`).
- `@lionlang/typesafe-ai` (v0.1.0): Bindings for TypeSafe AI's Jev judgment primitives (`typesafe/noul`, `typesafe/choice`, `typesafe/score`, `typesafe/system-one`).

## Quick Start

### TypeScript / Effect

```bash
npm install @lionlang/core effect
# or: bun add @lionlang/core effect
```

```ts
import { Effect } from "effect";
import { run } from "@lionlang/core/evaluation/evaluate";
import { stdlib } from "@lionlang/core/modules";

const result = await Effect.runPromise(
  run(["number/add", 1, 2], { ...stdlib, taxRate: 0.08 })
);
```

### CLI

```bash
npx @lionlang/cli -e '["number/add", 1, 2]'
npx @lionlang/cli check program.json
npx @lionlang/cli setup.json --database store.json
npx @lionlang/cli inspect store.json --derived
npx @lionlang/cli diff before.json after.json --derived
npx @lionlang/cli repl
npx @lionlang/cli worker > lion-worker.js
```

## Agent Skills

Install Lion's official agent skills into Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, or any skills-compatible agent:

```bash
npx skills add andrueandersoncs/lion
```

- **lion-research** (https://github.com/andrueandersoncs/lion/tree/main/skills/lion-research): Turn deep research, due diligence, or incident timelines into a proof-building Lion logic model with verbatim source quotes, contradiction/restatement detection, exact solver bounds, and a self-contained interactive `explorer.html`.
- **lion-reasoning** (https://github.com/andrueandersoncs/lion/tree/main/skills/lion-reasoning): Content-hashed working memory for coding agents — tracks observations against file hashes, detects stale evidence and contradicted hypotheses across long debugging, auditing, or optimization sessions.

## High-Leverage Use Cases

1. **Dynamic App Config & Validation**: Store schemas, pricing rules, and validation lambdas in Postgres JSONB or Git. Validate user-authored rules with `lion check`, evaluate in-memory on Effect, and edit visually in Fold Map.
2. **Verifiable Authorization & Business Policies**: Express RBAC/ReBAC and compliance rules in Datalog + lambdas. Get exact `why` explanations for every allow/deny, test changes with `assuming`, enforce `invariant`s, and formally prove universal properties with `proof/prove` + `proof/valid?`.
3. **Knowledge Bases, Ontologies & Deep Research Artifacts**: Model entities, relations, and quoted claims. Run `graph/pageRank`, `graph/shortestPath`, `graph/cycles`, `graph/dominators`, and `graph/influence`; measure epistemic fragility with `proof/sensitivity`; save via `snapshot`; ship live browser artifacts with `lion worker`.
4. **Safe Logic for AI Agents**: Have LLMs emit JSON Lion programs instead of raw JS/Python; verify with `lion check`; use `proof/bounds` and `proof/prove` for exact math/constraints; combine with `@lionlang/typesafe-ai` for hybrid neural-symbolic workflows.

## Documentation

### Tutorials

- [Your first Lion program](https://lionlang.dev/docs.html#first-program): Build a small checkout calculator, one working step at a time, and learn how Lion reads JSON as code along the way.
- [Build a family tree](https://lionlang.dev/docs.html#family-tree): Store facts about a family, then ask Lion's logic database to work out grandparents, ancestors, and more, all in JSON.
- [Run an order desk](https://lionlang.dev/docs.html#order-desk): Track orders whose status changes over time, keep the data consistent with an invariant, and save the whole desk as a Lion program.
- [Sort an inbox](https://lionlang.dev/docs.html#sort-an-inbox): Describe the orders you expect with a schema, find what is wrong with the ones that do not fit, and let rules take the good ones apart.

### How-to guides

- [Run Lion from TypeScript](https://lionlang.dev/docs.html#run-from-typescript): Evaluate Lion programs inside your own application, give them your values and functions, and handle their results and errors.
- [Run programs from the command line](https://lionlang.dev/docs.html#use-the-cli): Evaluate Lion files with the lion command, keep a logic database in a file between runs, and open the graph editor.
- [Branch on a value's shape](https://lionlang.dev/docs.html#branch-on-shape): Choose what to do with a value based on its type or its structure, with match and cond.
- [Transform lists](https://lionlang.dev/docs.html#transform-lists): Make lists, map over them, filter them, flatten them, and fold them into a single value.
- [Build and run code as data](https://lionlang.dev/docs.html#code-as-data): Hold a program as data, assemble one from parts, and run it with eval.
- [Query with conditions and computed values](https://lionlang.dev/docs.html#query-with-conditions): Narrow answers with comparisons, compute new values in rules and queries, choose between values, combine alternatives, and look inside lists.
- [Use answers as values](https://lionlang.dev/docs.html#ask-questions): Ask the database from any expression: collect answers into a list with find, test a goal in cond, and use a relation as a predicate.
- [Sort, page, and check query answers](https://lionlang.dev/docs.html#sort-and-page): Order answers by one or more variables, take a page of them, and make a query fail when it finds too few or too many.
- [Follow relationships of any length](https://lionlang.dev/docs.html#recursive-relations): Derive paths, reachability, and hierarchies with recursive rules, and write them so queries stay fast.
- [Find what is missing](https://lionlang.dev/docs.html#find-missing): Ask for things that have no matching fact, such as customers without orders or tasks without an owner.
- [Say that something exists](https://lionlang.dev/docs.html#say-something-exists): Write rules that say a value exists without saying what it is, read the unknowns they invent, keep only known answers, and make unknowns one with a key or an equality rule.
- [Summarize groups of facts](https://lionlang.dev/docs.html#summarize-groups): Count, total, average, and collect values per group, like GROUP BY in SQL.
- [Answer graph questions](https://lionlang.dev/docs.html#graph-questions): Find shortest routes, rank nodes, group connected nodes, detect cycles, and order dependencies with the graph module.
- [Enforce rules on your data](https://lionlang.dev/docs.html#enforce-rules): State conditions your data must always meet, and have the database refuse any change that would break them.
- [Solve for values and prove rules](https://lionlang.dev/docs.html#solve-for-values): Let a schema type a variable no goal binds, and Lion solves for the values that meet your filters, says whether one exists, or proves that none does, for every number; what it cannot decide waits for the values it lists.
- [Check every run of commands](https://lionlang.dev/docs.html#check-every-run): Ask about every run of commands up to a length, and the states each passes through: a rule that must always hold, something that must eventually happen, and the shortest run that breaks a rule, with amounts of any size the solver works out.
- [Prove that every command keeps a rule](https://lionlang.dev/docs.html#prove-commands): Prove for every state and every command that a step keeps a rule, see a state that breaks the proof, find the rules a proof needs, check a proof's certificate yourself, and ask whether one schema includes another.
- [Check the shape of data](https://lionlang.dev/docs.html#check-data): Say what a value must be with a schema, find where data does not fit, and have a relation refuse rows that do not.
- [Take data apart](https://lionlang.dev/docs.html#take-data-apart): Bind logic variables to the parts of records and lists with patterns, in relation calls, queries, and rules.
- [Explain a result](https://lionlang.dev/docs.html#explain-results): Find out why a fact holds: which rule derived it, from which facts, all the way down. Or why it does not: which rules could have given it, and what stopped each one.
- [Save and load a logic database](https://lionlang.dev/docs.html#save-and-load): Write a database out as a Lion program, store it anywhere, and rebuild it later from the command line or TypeScript.
- [Add your own functions and algorithms](https://lionlang.dev/docs.html#extend-with-host-code): Give Lion programs your own values and functions, use them inside logic rules, and add graph-style algorithms.
- [Call JavaScript objects and methods](https://lionlang.dev/docs.html#call-host-objects): Read properties, call methods, construct classes, and pass Lion functions to JavaScript callbacks.
- [Ask AI models with TypeSafe](https://lionlang.dev/docs.html#ask-ai-models): Turn natural language into typed judgments inside a Lion program with the TypeSafe AI and Jev bindings.

### Reference

- [Evaluation rules](https://lionlang.dev/docs.html#evaluation-rules): How Lion evaluates each kind of JSON value: numbers, booleans, null, strings, arrays, and records.
- [Special forms](https://lionlang.dev/docs.html#special-forms): The forms that control evaluation: quote, eval, begin, define, set!, lambda, cond, and match.
- [Logic forms](https://lionlang.dev/docs.html#logic-forms): The forms of Lion's Datalog-style logic layer: relations, facts, rules, queries, goals, questions, unknowns, snapshots, and invariants.
- [Query options](https://lionlang.dev/docs.html#query-options): The options record of a query: order, offset, limit, and assert, and the order Lion sorts values in.
- [Standard library](https://lionlang.dev/docs.html#standard-library): Every function in Lion's default environment, by module: number, boolean, string, array, value, schema, object, func, console, aggregate, and graph.
- [Logic database guarantees](https://lionlang.dev/docs.html#logic-guarantees): The rules every logic program follows, what Lion checks and when, and what it promises about changes and answers.
- [Errors](https://lionlang.dev/docs.html#errors): Every way a Lion program can fail, the error's tag, and what causes it.
- [Command line](https://lionlang.dev/docs.html#cli): The lion command from @lionlang/cli: evaluating files, keeping a database file, serving the graph editor, and printing Lion as a Web Worker.
- [TypeScript API](https://lionlang.dev/docs.html#typescript-api): The exports of @lionlang/core and @lionlang/typesafe-ai that host applications use.

### Explanation

- [Why programs are JSON](https://lionlang.dev/docs.html#why-json): What Lion gains by making every program a JSON value, what it costs, and how the evaluation rules make it work.
- [Names, scope, and environments](https://lionlang.dev/docs.html#names-and-scope): How Lion decides which strings are names, why a body declares what it defines from its start, and what lasts from one run to the next.
- [How Lion answers logic questions](https://lionlang.dev/docs.html#logic-programming): Why Lion's logic layer is Datalog rather than Prolog, how it computes answers bottom-up, and where its restrictions come from.
- [Goal-directed evaluation](https://lionlang.dev/docs.html#goal-directed-evaluation): How Lion avoids deriving everything a program implies when a query only needs a little, and why the shape of a recursive rule matters.
- [One set of rules for every feature](https://lionlang.dev/docs.html#consistent-semantics): Why Lion's features share the same few rules, how that follows from the principle of least astonishment, and how Lion settles the places where JavaScript and JSON disagree.

## Lion documentation

URL: https://lionlang.dev/docs.html#overview
Section: Overview (Overview)

> Everything Lion can do, organized by what you need right now: to learn, to get a job done, to look something up, or to understand why.

Lion is a small Lisp whose programs are JSON. It evaluates on Effect, edits as a graph, runs from the command line, and includes a Datalog-style logic database.

These docs follow the [Diátaxis](https://diataxis.fr/) framework. There are four kinds of documentation, each written for a different need, and they are kept apart so each one can do its own job. Tutorials teach and how-to guides direct; both are practical. Reference and explanation inform; both are theoretical.

### Where to start

- **New to Lion?** Take the tutorial [Your first Lion program](https://lionlang.dev/docs.html#first-program). It takes about ten minutes, and every step runs in your browser.
- **Have a job to do?** Pick a how-to guide, such as [Run Lion from TypeScript](https://lionlang.dev/docs.html#run-from-typescript), [Check the shape of data](https://lionlang.dev/docs.html#check-data), or [Enforce rules on your data](https://lionlang.dev/docs.html#enforce-rules).
- **Need an exact answer?** The reference describes every [special form](https://lionlang.dev/docs.html#special-forms), [logic form](https://lionlang.dev/docs.html#logic-forms), [standard library function](https://lionlang.dev/docs.html#standard-library), and [command](https://lionlang.dev/docs.html#cli).
- **Wondering why Lion works the way it does?** Start with [Why programs are JSON](https://lionlang.dev/docs.html#why-json).

### Every example is live

A program with a result under it is a live example. Edit the program and it runs again; press `⌘`/`Ctrl` + `Enter` to run it at once, or Reset to bring back the original.

**Example: Try it**

```json
["number/multiply", ["number/add", 1, 2], 4]
```

Result:

```json
12
```

Examples run in your browser on the same evaluator as `@lionlang/core`. Each one starts from the standard library, a fresh environment, and an empty logic database, so examples never affect each other. The results printed on this page were computed by that evaluator when the docs were built.

Press `/` anywhere to search. Search finds documents, sections, and every form and function by name.

---

## Your first Lion program

URL: https://lionlang.dev/docs.html#first-program
Section: Tutorials (Tutorial)

> Build a small checkout calculator, one working step at a time, and learn how Lion reads JSON as code along the way.

In this tutorial we will build a checkout calculator: given a cart total, it applies a discount for large orders and reports what the customer pays. Each step adds one idea and runs right here, so you can see every result as you go. You don't need to install anything.

### Step 1: Write a value

Every Lion program is JSON. Start with the simplest program there is, a number. Edit it to any other number and watch the result follow.

**Example: A value**

```json
42
```

Result:

```json
42
```

A record is a program too. Lion evaluates each of its values and keeps its keys:

**Example: A record**

```json
{"item": "lamp", "price": 120, "inStock": true}
```

Result:

```json
{"item":"lamp","price":120,"inStock":true}
```

Numbers, booleans, `null`, and records of them come back as they are.

### Step 2: Call a function

An array is a call. Its first element names the function, and the rest are its arguments. Add two prices:

**Example: A call**

```json
["number/add", 120, 35]
```

Result:

```json
155
```

The name `number/add` comes from Lion's standard library, which groups functions by module: `number/`, `string/`, `array/`, and so on.

### Step 3: Nest calls

An argument can be another call. Lion evaluates the inner call first and passes its result on. Here is the cart total with 10% taken off:

**Example: Nested calls**

```json
["number/multiply",
  ["number/add", 120, 35],
  0.9]
```

Result:

```json
139.5
```

### Step 4: Name a value

To use the total more than once, give it a name with `define`. To run several steps in order, wrap them in `begin`, which returns the last result:

**Example: Naming a value**

```json
["begin",
  ["define", "total", ["number/add", 120, 35]],
  ["number/multiply", "total", 0.9]]
```

Result:

```json
139.5
```

Notice that the string `"total"` now stands for 155. A string that names something evaluates to what it names.

### Step 5: Write a function

A `lambda` is a function you write yourself: a list of parameter names and a body. Define one that applies a discount rate to any amount:

**Example: A function**

```json
["begin",
  ["define", "discounted",
    ["lambda", ["amount", "rate"],
      ["number/multiply", "amount", ["number/subtract", 1, "rate"]]]],
  ["discounted", 155, 0.1]]
```

Result:

```json
139.5
```

Change `0.1` to `0.25` and the result changes with it.

### Step 6: Make a decision

Only large orders get the discount. `cond` checks conditions in order and returns the result next to the first one that holds:

**Example: A decision**

```json
["begin",
  ["define", "total", 155],
  ["cond",
    [["number/greaterThan", "total", 100], "discount"],
    ["else", "full price"]]]
```

Result:

```json
"discount"
```

Try a total of `80`.

### Step 7: Put it together

Now combine everything into the calculator. A function that takes a list of prices adds them up, works out the discount, and returns a record, so the result shows each part of the checkout:

**Example: Checkout calculator**

```json
["begin",
  ["define", "rate",
    ["lambda", ["total"],
      ["cond",
        [["number/greaterThan", "total", 100], 0.1],
        ["else", 0]]]],
  ["define", "receipt",
    ["lambda", ["total"],
      {"total": "total",
       "discount": ["number/multiply", "total", ["rate", "total"]],
       "pay": ["number/multiply", "total", ["number/subtract", 1, ["rate", "total"]]]}]],
  ["define", "checkout",
    ["lambda", ["prices"],
      ["receipt", ["aggregate/sum", "prices"]]]],
  ["checkout", ["array/make", 120, 35]]]
```

Result:

```json
{"total":155,"discount":15.5,"pay":139.5}
```

Change the prices in `["array/make", 120, 35]` to `40, 35` and the discount disappears.

### What we built

We wrote a working program in plain JSON. Along the way we used values, calls, names, functions, decisions, and records, which is most of the core language. Because the program is JSON, you could store it in a database, send it over HTTP, or have another program write it.

Next, the tutorial [Build a family tree](https://lionlang.dev/docs.html#family-tree) uses the same JSON to ask questions of a logic database. To look up the forms used here, see [Special forms](https://lionlang.dev/docs.html#special-forms); to learn how names work, read [Names, scope, and environments](https://lionlang.dev/docs.html#names-and-scope).

---

## Build a family tree

URL: https://lionlang.dev/docs.html#family-tree
Section: Tutorials (Tutorial)

> Store facts about a family, then ask Lion's logic database to work out grandparents, ancestors, and more, all in JSON.

In this tutorial we will record a small family and let Lion's logic database answer questions about it: who is whose grandparent, who descends from whom, and who has no children yet. At the end we will protect the tree from impossible data.

Each step shows the whole program so far, because every example runs on its own. New lines are at the end.

### Step 1: Declare a relation and add facts

A relation is a table with named columns. Declare `parent`, then add four facts to it. The `fact` form returns the facts it added:

**Example: Facts**

```json
["begin",
  ["relation", "parent", ["parent", "child"]],
  ["fact",
    ["parent", "ada", "bea"],
    ["parent", "ada", "cal"],
    ["parent", "bea", "dot"],
    ["parent", "dot", "eli"]]]
```

Result:

```json
[
  ["parent","ada","bea"],
  ["parent","ada","cal"],
  ["parent","bea","dot"],
  ["parent","dot","eli"]
]
```

### Step 2: Ask a question

A `query` asks for every way to fill in the strings that start with `?`. Those are logic variables. Ask who Ada's children are:

**Example: A query**

```json
["begin",
  ["relation", "parent", ["parent", "child"]],
  ["fact",
    ["parent", "ada", "bea"],
    ["parent", "ada", "cal"],
    ["parent", "bea", "dot"],
    ["parent", "dot", "eli"]],
  ["query", ["parent", "ada", "?child"]]]
```

Result:

```json
[{"child":"bea"},{"child":"cal"}]
```

There is one answer per child, keyed by the variable's name. Try `["parent", "?who", "dot"]` to ask who Dot's parent is.

### Step 3: Write a rule

A rule derives new facts. A grandparent is a parent of a parent, so the rule says: `?g` is a grandparent of `?c` when `?g` is a parent of some `?p` and `?p` is a parent of `?c`.

**Example: A rule**

```json
["begin",
  ["relation", "parent", ["parent", "child"]],
  ["relation", "grandparent", ["grandparent", "child"]],
  ["fact",
    ["parent", "ada", "bea"],
    ["parent", "ada", "cal"],
    ["parent", "bea", "dot"],
    ["parent", "dot", "eli"]],
  ["rule", ["grandparent", "?g", "?c"],
    ["parent", "?g", "?p"],
    ["parent", "?p", "?c"]],
  ["query", ["grandparent", "?g", "?c"]]]
```

Result:

```json
[{"g":"ada","c":"dot"},{"g":"bea","c":"eli"}]
```

### Step 4: Follow the line all the way back

An ancestor is a parent, or an ancestor of a parent. A relation can refer to itself, so two rules cover both cases:

**Example: Recursive rules**

```json
["begin",
  ["relation", "parent", ["parent", "child"]],
  ["relation", "ancestor", ["ancestor", "person"]],
  ["fact",
    ["parent", "ada", "bea"],
    ["parent", "ada", "cal"],
    ["parent", "bea", "dot"],
    ["parent", "dot", "eli"]],
  ["rule", ["ancestor", "?a", "?p"], ["parent", "?a", "?p"]],
  ["rule", ["ancestor", "?a", "?p"],
    ["ancestor", "?a", "?mid"],
    ["parent", "?mid", "?p"]],
  ["query", ["ancestor", "?who", "eli"], {"order": "who"}]]
```

Result:

```json
[{"who":"ada"},{"who":"bea"},{"who":"dot"}]
```

Eli's ancestors come back sorted, because the query asked for `{"order": "who"}`.

### Step 5: Ask what is missing

Who has no children? Declare who is in the family, then use `not` to keep only the people with no `parent` fact of their own. `?_` means "anything, I don't care what":

**Example: Negation**

```json
["begin",
  ["relation", "person", ["name"]],
  ["relation", "parent", ["parent", "child"]],
  ["relation", "childless", ["name"]],
  ["fact", ["person", "ada"], ["person", "bea"], ["person", "cal"],
    ["person", "dot"], ["person", "eli"]],
  ["fact",
    ["parent", "ada", "bea"],
    ["parent", "ada", "cal"],
    ["parent", "bea", "dot"],
    ["parent", "dot", "eli"]],
  ["rule", ["childless", "?p"],
    ["person", "?p"],
    ["not", ["parent", "?p", "?_"]]],
  ["query", ["childless", "?name"]]]
```

Result:

```json
[{"name":"cal"},{"name":"eli"}]
```

### Step 6: Count descendants

A rule can count. Put `aggregate/count` in the rule's head, and Lion counts the matches for each ancestor:

**Example: Counting**

```json
["begin",
  ["relation", "parent", ["parent", "child"]],
  ["relation", "ancestor", ["ancestor", "person"]],
  ["relation", "descendants", ["ancestor", "count"]],
  ["fact",
    ["parent", "ada", "bea"],
    ["parent", "ada", "cal"],
    ["parent", "bea", "dot"],
    ["parent", "dot", "eli"]],
  ["rule", ["ancestor", "?a", "?p"], ["parent", "?a", "?p"]],
  ["rule", ["ancestor", "?a", "?p"],
    ["ancestor", "?a", "?mid"],
    ["parent", "?mid", "?p"]],
  ["rule", ["descendants", "?a", ["aggregate/count", "?p"]],
    ["ancestor", "?a", "?p"]],
  ["query", ["descendants", "?ancestor", "?count"], {"order": "-count"}]]
```

Result:

```json
[
  {"ancestor":"ada","count":4},
  {"ancestor":"bea","count":2},
  {"ancestor":"dot","count":1}
]
```

### Step 7: Collect answers into a list

A query gives one record per answer. To put answers inside a value of our own, we use `find`: it takes a template and a goal, and returns the template's value for every match, as a sorted list. Here the template is a pair, a person and the list of their children, and that list is a `find` too:

**Example: Find**

```json
["begin",
  ["relation", "person", ["name"]],
  ["relation", "parent", ["parent", "child"]],
  ["fact", ["person", "ada"], ["person", "bea"], ["person", "cal"],
    ["person", "dot"], ["person", "eli"]],
  ["fact",
    ["parent", "ada", "bea"],
    ["parent", "ada", "cal"],
    ["parent", "bea", "dot"],
    ["parent", "dot", "eli"]],
  ["find",
    ["array/make", "?p", ["find", "?child", ["parent", "?p", "?child"]]],
    ["person", "?p"]]]
```

Result:

```json
[
  ["ada",["bea","cal"]],
  ["bea",["dot"]],
  ["cal",[]],
  ["dot",["eli"]],
  ["eli",[]]
]
```

The inner `find` is asked once for each person. Cal and Eli have no children, so they get an empty list instead of being left out, which the count in step 6 could not do.

### Step 8: Ask why

`why` explains a fact: which rule produced it, and from which facts. Ask why Ada is an ancestor of Eli:

**Example: Why**

```json
["begin",
  ["relation", "parent", ["parent", "child"]],
  ["relation", "ancestor", ["ancestor", "person"]],
  ["fact",
    ["parent", "ada", "bea"],
    ["parent", "bea", "dot"],
    ["parent", "dot", "eli"]],
  ["rule", ["ancestor", "?a", "?p"], ["parent", "?a", "?p"]],
  ["rule", ["ancestor", "?a", "?p"],
    ["ancestor", "?a", "?mid"],
    ["parent", "?mid", "?p"]],
  ["why", ["ancestor", "ada", "eli"]]]
```

Result:

```json
{
  "fact": ["ancestor","ada","eli"],
  "rule": [
    "rule",
    ["ancestor","?a","?p"],
    ["ancestor","?a","?mid"],
    ["parent","?mid","?p"]
  ],
  "because": [
    {
      "fact": ["ancestor","ada","dot"],
      "rule": [
        "rule",
        ["ancestor","?a","?p"],
        ["ancestor","?a","?mid"],
        ["parent","?mid","?p"]
      ],
      "because": [
        {
          "fact": ["ancestor","ada","bea"],
          "rule": ["rule",["ancestor","?a","?p"],["parent","?a","?p"]],
          "because": [{"fact":["parent","ada","bea"],"given":true}]
        },
        {"fact":["parent","bea","dot"],"given":true}
      ]
    },
    {"fact":["parent","dot","eli"],"given":true}
  ]
}
```

Read it from the outside in: Ada is an ancestor of Eli because she is an ancestor of Dot, who is Eli's parent, and so on down to facts that were given.

### Step 9: Protect the tree

Nobody can be their own ancestor. An `invariant` tells the database a question that must never have an answer. Add it, then try a fact that would make Eli Ada's parent:

**Example: An invariant**

```json
["begin",
  ["relation", "parent", ["parent", "child"]],
  ["relation", "ancestor", ["ancestor", "person"]],
  ["fact",
    ["parent", "ada", "bea"],
    ["parent", "bea", "dot"],
    ["parent", "dot", "eli"]],
  ["rule", ["ancestor", "?a", "?p"], ["parent", "?a", "?p"]],
  ["rule", ["ancestor", "?a", "?p"],
    ["ancestor", "?a", "?mid"],
    ["parent", "?mid", "?p"]],
  ["invariant", ["ancestor", "?x", "?x"], {"assert": "none"}],
  ["fact", ["parent", "eli", "ada"]]]
```

Error:

```text
LogicError: Adding this fact breaks an invariant, so nothing changed. The invariant expected no answers but found 4, such as {"x":"ada"}: ["ancestor","?x","?x"].
```

The database refuses the fact and tells us why: with it, Ada would be her own ancestor. The tree stays as it was. Change the last fact to `["parent", "eli", "fay"]` and the program succeeds.

### What we built

We stored facts, derived new ones with rules, followed a relationship through any number of generations, asked about what was missing, counted, collected answers into lists, explained an answer, and guarded the data with an invariant. Every part was plain JSON.

Next, [Run an order desk](https://lionlang.dev/docs.html#order-desk) keeps changing data consistent over time. For every logic form and its exact rules, see [Logic forms](https://lionlang.dev/docs.html#logic-forms); to learn how the database computes answers, read [How Lion answers logic questions](https://lionlang.dev/docs.html#logic-programming).

---

## Run an order desk

URL: https://lionlang.dev/docs.html#order-desk
Section: Tutorials (Tutorial)

> Track orders whose status changes over time, keep the data consistent with an invariant, and save the whole desk as a Lion program.

In this tutorial we will run a small order desk. Orders change status as they move along, the desk refuses changes that would leave the data inconsistent, and at the end we save everything to a file. We will build on the logic forms from [Build a family tree](https://lionlang.dev/docs.html#family-tree).

### Step 1: Keep one row per order

Each order has an id, a customer, a status, and an amount. Give the relation a key, `{"key": "id"}`, so it holds at most one row per id:

**Example: A keyed relation**

```json
["begin",
  ["relation", "order", ["id", "customer", "status", "amount"], {"key": "id"}],
  ["fact",
    ["order", 1, "ana", "open", 30],
    ["order", 2, "ana", "open", 20],
    ["order", 3, "bo", "open", 50]],
  ["query", ["order", "?id", "?customer", "?status", "?amount"], {"order": "id"}]]
```

Result:

```json
[
  {"id":1,"customer":"ana","status":"open","amount":30},
  {"id":2,"customer":"ana","status":"open","amount":20},
  {"id":3,"customer":"bo","status":"open","amount":50}
]
```

### Step 2: Change an order's status

To move order 1 along, add a fact with the same id. Because `id` is the key, the new row replaces the old one instead of sitting next to it:

**Example: An update**

```json
["begin",
  ["relation", "order", ["id", "customer", "status", "amount"], {"key": "id"}],
  ["fact",
    ["order", 1, "ana", "open", 30],
    ["order", 2, "ana", "open", 20],
    ["order", 3, "bo", "open", 50]],
  ["fact", ["order", 1, "ana", "paid", 30]],
  ["query", ["order", "?id", "?customer", "?status", "?amount"], {"order": "id"}]]
```

Result:

```json
[
  {"id":1,"customer":"ana","status":"paid","amount":30},
  {"id":2,"customer":"ana","status":"open","amount":20},
  {"id":3,"customer":"bo","status":"open","amount":50}
]
```

### Step 3: Total what each customer owes

A rule with `aggregate/sum` in its head adds up the amounts of each customer's open orders:

**Example: A running total**

```json
["begin",
  ["relation", "order", ["id", "customer", "status", "amount"], {"key": "id"}],
  ["relation", "owed", ["customer", "total"]],
  ["fact",
    ["order", 1, "ana", "paid", 30],
    ["order", 2, "ana", "open", 20],
    ["order", 3, "bo", "open", 50]],
  ["rule", ["owed", "?c", ["aggregate/sum", "?amount"]],
    ["order", "?_", "?c", "open", "?amount"]],
  ["query", ["owed", "?customer", "?total"], {"order": "customer"}]]
```

Result:

```json
[{"customer":"ana","total":20},{"customer":"bo","total":50}]
```

Change order 3 to `"paid"`, and Bo drops out of the answer.

### Step 4: Refuse to ship without an address

An order must not ship to a customer without an address. Store addresses, and add an invariant: a question that must never have an answer. Then try to ship Bo's order:

**Example: An invariant**

```json
["begin",
  ["relation", "order", ["id", "customer", "status", "amount"], {"key": "id"}],
  ["relation", "address", ["customer", "street"], {"key": "customer"}],
  ["fact",
    ["order", 1, "ana", "paid", 30],
    ["order", 3, "bo", "open", 50]],
  ["fact", ["address", "ana", "1 Elm St"]],
  ["invariant",
    ["and", ["order", "?id", "?c", "shipped", "?_"], ["not", ["address", "?c", "?_"]]],
    {"assert": "none"}],
  ["fact", ["order", 3, "bo", "shipped", 50]]]
```

Error:

```text
LogicError: Adding this fact breaks an invariant, so nothing changed. The invariant expected no answers but found 1, such as {"id":3,"c":"bo"}: ["and",["order","?id","?c","shipped","?_"],["not",["address","?c","?_"]]].
```

The desk refuses: the change would ship order 3 to a customer with no address. Nothing changed, so order 3 is still open.

### Step 5: Make both changes at once

Bo sends an address. A single `fact` form can add the address and ship the order together. The invariant is checked once the whole form is done, so this succeeds:

**Example: One change, two facts**

```json
["begin",
  ["relation", "order", ["id", "customer", "status", "amount"], {"key": "id"}],
  ["relation", "address", ["customer", "street"], {"key": "customer"}],
  ["fact",
    ["order", 1, "ana", "paid", 30],
    ["order", 3, "bo", "open", 50]],
  ["fact", ["address", "ana", "1 Elm St"]],
  ["invariant",
    ["and", ["order", "?id", "?c", "shipped", "?_"], ["not", ["address", "?c", "?_"]]],
    {"assert": "none"}],
  ["fact", ["address", "bo", "9 Oak Ave"], ["order", 3, "bo", "shipped", 50]],
  ["query", ["order", "?id", "?customer", "?status", "?_"], {"order": "id"}]]
```

Result:

```json
[
  {"id":1,"customer":"ana","status":"paid"},
  {"id":3,"customer":"bo","status":"shipped"}
]
```

### Step 6: Save the desk

`["snapshot"]` writes the whole database as a Lion program: its relations, facts, and invariant. Running that program rebuilds the desk exactly.

**Example: A snapshot**

```json
["begin",
  ["relation", "order", ["id", "customer", "status", "amount"], {"key": "id"}],
  ["relation", "address", ["customer", "street"], {"key": "customer"}],
  ["fact", ["order", 1, "ana", "paid", 30], ["order", 3, "bo", "shipped", 50]],
  ["fact", ["address", "ana", "1 Elm St"], ["address", "bo", "9 Oak Ave"]],
  ["invariant",
    ["and", ["order", "?id", "?c", "shipped", "?_"], ["not", ["address", "?c", "?_"]]],
    {"assert": "none"}],
  ["snapshot"]]
```

Result:

```json
[
  "begin",
  [
    "relation",
    "order",
    ["id","customer","status","amount"],
    {"key":["id"]}
  ],
  [
    "relation",
    "address",
    ["customer","street"],
    {"key":["customer"]}
  ],
  [
    "fact",
    ["order",1,"ana","paid",30],
    ["order",3,"bo","shipped",50],
    ["address","ana","1 Elm St"],
    ["address","bo","9 Oak Ave"]
  ],
  [
    "invariant",
    [
      "and",
      ["order","?id","?c","shipped","?_"],
      ["not",["address","?c","?_"]]
    ],
    {"assert":"none"}
  ]
]
```

On your own machine, the `lion` command does this for you. Save the program from Step 5 as `desk.json` and run it with a database file; later programs then run against the saved desk, and the invariant still guards it:

```shell
bun add --dev @lionlang/cli
bun run lion desk.json --database store.json
```

### What we built

We kept one row per order with a key, changed statuses by adding facts, totaled what customers owe, refused an inconsistent change with an invariant, made two changes together, and saved the desk as a Lion program.

To use these features in your own project, see [Enforce rules on your data](https://lionlang.dev/docs.html#enforce-rules) and [Save and load a logic database](https://lionlang.dev/docs.html#save-and-load). To understand why a change is all or nothing, read [One set of rules for every feature](https://lionlang.dev/docs.html#consistent-semantics).

---

## Sort an inbox

URL: https://lionlang.dev/docs.html#sort-an-inbox
Section: Tutorials (Tutorial)

> Describe the orders you expect with a schema, find what is wrong with the ones that do not fit, and let rules take the good ones apart.

In this tutorial we will sort an inbox of orders that arrive as JSON. Some are well formed and some are not. We will say what an order must be, see exactly where a bad one goes wrong, and write rules that keep the good ones and take them apart. We will build on the logic forms from [Build a family tree](https://lionlang.dev/docs.html#family-tree).

### Step 1: Say what an order is

A schema says what a value must be, and anything can be one. Write the record we expect, with a schema in place of each value: a function such as `value/integer?` for a value it accepts, and `schema/anyOf` for a choice. `schema/fits?` asks whether a value fits:

**Example: A schema**

```json
["begin",
  ["define", "Order",
    {"id": "value/integer?",
     "status": ["schema/anyOf", "open", "shipped"],
     "lines": ["schema/arrayOf",
       {"sku": "value/string?", "qty": "value/integer?"}]}],
  ["define", "mail",
    ["quote", {"id": 1, "status": "open", "lines": [{"sku": "tea", "qty": 2}]}]],
  ["schema/fits?", "mail", "Order"]]
```

Result:

```json
true
```

The order fits: it has the three keys, and each value fits the schema under its key.

### Step 2: Find what is wrong

The next order in the mail is a mess. `schema/problems` lists every place where a value does not fit:

**Example: Problems**

```json
["begin",
  ["define", "Order",
    {"id": "value/integer?",
     "status": ["schema/anyOf", "open", "shipped"],
     "lines": ["schema/arrayOf",
       {"sku": "value/string?", "qty": "value/integer?"}]}],
  ["define", "mail",
    ["quote", {"id": "2", "status": "opne", "lines": [{"sku": "tea"}], "gift": true}]],
  ["schema/problems", "mail", "Order"]]
```

Result:

```json
[
  {"path":["gift"],"found":true},
  {"path":["id"],"expected":"value/integer?","found":"2"},
  {"path":["lines",0,"qty"],"expected":"value/integer?"},
  {
    "path": ["status"],
    "expected": ["schema/anyOf","open","shipped"],
    "found": "opne"
  }
]
```

There are four. Each has the `path` to the part that is wrong. The `id` and the `status` have the wrong value, so they show what was `expected` and what was `found`. The first line has no `qty`, so it shows only what was expected. And `gift` is a key the schema does not name, so it shows only what was found: a record fits a record with the same keys.

### Step 3: Give the schemas names

`schema` declares a schema under a name, the way `relation` declares a relation. The name is then a predicate, and other schemas can use it. Let us also ask for more: a quantity must be above zero, which a lambda can say, and an order may have a note, which `schema/optional` allows:

**Example: Named schemas**

```json
["begin",
  ["schema", "Line",
    {"sku": "value/string?",
     "qty": ["schema/allOf", "value/integer?",
       ["lambda", ["n"], ["number/greaterThan", "n", 0]]]}],
  ["schema", "Order",
    {"id": "value/integer?",
     "status": ["schema/anyOf", "open", "shipped"],
     "lines": ["schema/arrayOf", "Line"],
     "note": ["schema/optional", "value/string?"]}],
  {"with a note": ["Order",
     ["quote", {"id": 1, "status": "open", "lines": [], "note": "gift"}]],
   "no tea": ["Order",
     ["quote", {"id": 1, "status": "open", "lines": [{"sku": "tea", "qty": 0}]}]]}]
```

Result:

```json
{"with a note":true,"no tea":false}
```

Change the `0` to a `3`, and the second order fits too.

### Step 4: Keep the orders that fit

Now put the mail in a relation, one document per row. A relation call takes a schema for each column, so `["inbox", "Order"]` would ask for the rows that are orders. We want more than that: the id and the status of each. A logic variable in a schema takes the value it meets, so a record with variables in it is a pattern. `schema/allOf` asks for both at once, and `schema/open` lets the pattern name only the keys it wants:

**Example: A rule that sorts**

```json
["begin",
  ["schema", "Line",
    {"sku": "value/string?",
     "qty": ["schema/allOf", "value/integer?",
       ["lambda", ["n"], ["number/greaterThan", "n", 0]]]}],
  ["schema", "Order",
    {"id": "value/integer?",
     "status": ["schema/anyOf", "open", "shipped"],
     "lines": ["schema/arrayOf", "Line"]}],
  ["relation", "inbox", ["doc"]],
  ["relation", "order", ["id", "status"], {"key": "id"}],
  ["fact",
    ["inbox", ["quote", {"id": 1, "status": "open",
      "lines": [{"sku": "tea", "qty": 2}, {"sku": "cup", "qty": 1}]}]],
    ["inbox", ["quote", {"id": 2, "status": "opne", "lines": []}]],
    ["inbox", ["quote", {"id": 3, "status": "shipped",
      "lines": [{"sku": "tea", "qty": 5}]}]]],
  ["rule", ["order", "?id", "?status"],
    ["inbox", ["schema/allOf", "Order",
      ["schema/open", {"id": "?id", "status": "?status"}]]]],
  ["query", ["order", "?id", "?status"], {"order": "id"}]]
```

Result:

```json
[{"id":1,"status":"open"},{"id":3,"status":"shipped"}]
```

Orders 1 and 3 are kept. Order 2 says `"opne"`, so it is not an order, and the rule passes over it.

### Step 5: Say why the rest was rejected

A document that was passed over should not vanish. `schema/problems` gives a list, and `in` turns a list into rows, so a second rule records each problem of each document:

**Example: A rule that explains**

```json
["begin",
  ["schema", "Line",
    {"sku": "value/string?",
     "qty": ["schema/allOf", "value/integer?",
       ["lambda", ["n"], ["number/greaterThan", "n", 0]]]}],
  ["schema", "Order",
    {"id": "value/integer?",
     "status": ["schema/anyOf", "open", "shipped"],
     "lines": ["schema/arrayOf", "Line"]}],
  ["relation", "inbox", ["doc"]],
  ["relation", "rejected", ["id", "where"]],
  ["fact",
    ["inbox", ["quote", {"id": 1, "status": "open",
      "lines": [{"sku": "tea", "qty": 2}, {"sku": "cup", "qty": 1}]}]],
    ["inbox", ["quote", {"id": 2, "status": "opne", "lines": []}]],
    ["inbox", ["quote", {"id": 4, "status": "open",
      "lines": [{"sku": "tea", "qty": 0}]}]]],
  ["rule", ["rejected", "?id", ["object/get", "?problem", "path"]],
    ["inbox", "?doc"],
    ["schema/fits?", "?doc", ["schema/open", {"id": "?id"}]],
    ["in", "?problem", ["schema/problems", "?doc", "Order"]]],
  ["query", ["rejected", "?id", "?where"], {"order": "id"}]]
```

Result:

```json
[{"id":2,"where":["status"]},{"id":4,"where":["lines",0,"qty"]}]
```

Order 1 has no problems, so it has no rows. Here `schema/fits?` is a goal of its own: it checks a value that another goal bound, and binds `?id` from it.

### Step 6: Take the lines apart

Each order holds a list of lines. The element of `in` can be a pattern too, so one goal takes the list out of the order and the next takes each line apart. With the lines as rows, an aggregate can total the units of each product:

**Example: Lines as rows**

```json
["begin",
  ["schema", "Line",
    {"sku": "value/string?",
     "qty": ["schema/allOf", "value/integer?",
       ["lambda", ["n"], ["number/greaterThan", "n", 0]]]}],
  ["schema", "Order",
    {"id": "value/integer?",
     "status": ["schema/anyOf", "open", "shipped"],
     "lines": ["schema/arrayOf", "Line"]}],
  ["relation", "inbox", ["doc"]],
  ["relation", "line", ["order", "sku", "qty"]],
  ["relation", "units", ["sku", "total"]],
  ["fact",
    ["inbox", ["quote", {"id": 1, "status": "open",
      "lines": [{"sku": "tea", "qty": 2}, {"sku": "cup", "qty": 1}]}]],
    ["inbox", ["quote", {"id": 2, "status": "opne", "lines": []}]],
    ["inbox", ["quote", {"id": 3, "status": "shipped",
      "lines": [{"sku": "tea", "qty": 5}]}]]],
  ["rule", ["line", "?order", "?sku", "?qty"],
    ["inbox", ["schema/allOf", "Order",
      ["schema/open", {"id": "?order", "lines": "?lines"}]]],
    ["in", {"sku": "?sku", "qty": "?qty"}, "?lines"]],
  ["rule", ["units", "?sku", ["aggregate/sum", "?qty"]],
    ["line", "?order", "?sku", "?qty"]],
  {"lines": ["find", ["array/make", "?order", "?sku", "?qty"],
     ["line", "?order", "?sku", "?qty"]],
   "units": ["query", ["units", "?sku", "?total"], {"order": "sku"}]}]
```

Result:

```json
{
  "lines": [[1,"cup",1],[1,"tea",2],[3,"tea",5]],
  "units": [{"sku":"cup","total":1},{"sku":"tea","total":7}]
}
```

### Step 7: Guard the shelf

The sorted orders live in a relation of their own. To make sure nothing else ever puts a bad row there, give the relation a schema. Every row, taken as a record of its columns, must then fit it, and a change that would add a row that does not is refused:

**Example: A guarded relation**

```json
["begin",
  ["schema", "Shelved",
    {"id": "value/integer?", "status": ["schema/anyOf", "open", "shipped"]}],
  ["relation", "order", ["id", "status"], {"key": "id", "schema": "Shelved"}],
  ["fact", ["order", 1, "open"], ["order", 3, "shipped"]],
  ["fact", ["order", 2, "opne"]]]
```

Error:

```text
LogicError: Adding this fact breaks an invariant, so nothing changed. The invariant expected no answers but found 1, such as {"id":2,"status":"opne"}: ["and",["order","?id","?status"],["not",["Shelved",{"id":"?id","status":"?status"}]]]. {"id":2,"status":"opne"} does not fit "Shelved": "status" must fit ["schema/anyOf","open","shipped"] but is "opne".
```

The message says which row does not fit, and where. Nothing changed: orders 1 and 3 are still on the shelf, and order 2 was not added.

### What we built

We described an order with a schema, listed the problems of one that did not fit, named our schemas, kept the documents that fit with a rule, recorded why the others were rejected, took a list inside each order apart into rows, and guarded a relation with a schema.

To use these features in your own project, see [Check the shape of data](https://lionlang.dev/docs.html#check-data) and [Take data apart](https://lionlang.dev/docs.html#take-data-apart). For every rule in one place, read [What fits a schema](https://lionlang.dev/docs.html#schema-fitting) and [Patterns](https://lionlang.dev/docs.html#logic-patterns) in the reference. To understand why checking and taking apart are one thing, read [One set of rules for every feature](https://lionlang.dev/docs.html#consistent-semantics).

---

## Run Lion from TypeScript

URL: https://lionlang.dev/docs.html#run-from-typescript
Section: How-to guides (How-to guide)

> Evaluate Lion programs inside your own application, give them your values and functions, and handle their results and errors.

This guide shows how to evaluate Lion from a TypeScript or JavaScript project with `@lionlang/core`. It assumes you know the basics of [Effect](https://effect.website); every evaluation is an Effect you run.

### Install the package

```shell
bun add @lionlang/core effect
```

### Evaluate a program

Pass the program and an environment to `run`. The standard library, `stdlib`, is the usual environment. A program can be any JSON value, so it can come straight from `JSON.parse`, a database, or a request body.

```ts
import { Effect } from "effect";
import { run } from "@lionlang/core/evaluation/evaluate";
import { stdlib } from "@lionlang/core/modules";

const program = JSON.parse('["number/add", 1, 2]');
const result = await Effect.runPromise(run(program, stdlib));
// => 3
```

### Give programs your own values and functions

Spread `stdlib` into an object and add names. Any value can be bound. A function can return a plain value or an Effect; Lion waits for an Effect to finish.

```ts
const env = {
  ...stdlib,
  taxRate: 0.08,
  "shop/price": (sku: string) => Effect.succeed(sku === "lamp" ? 120 : 35),
};

await Effect.runPromise(
  run(["number/multiply", ["shop/price", "lamp"], ["number/add", 1, "taxRate"]], env)
);
// => 129.6
```

Prefix your names with a module, as the standard library does, so they never collide with Lion's names or with strings in your data.

### Handle errors

A failed evaluation is a typed failure, not a thrown exception. Run with `Effect.runPromiseExit`, or catch by tag:

```ts
const safe = run(["number/add", "one", 2], stdlib).pipe(
  Effect.catchTag("LogicError", (error) => Effect.succeed(`Bad input: ${error.message}`))
);
```

See [Errors](https://lionlang.dev/docs.html#errors) for every error a program can fail with.

### Keep a logic database between runs

Each `run` starts with an empty logic database. To keep relations, facts, rules, and invariants across runs, create a `LogicDatabase` and pass it to each run:

```ts
import { LogicDatabase } from "@lionlang/core/logic/database";

const database = new LogicDatabase();
await Effect.runPromise(run(["begin",
  ["relation", "edge", ["from", "to"]],
  ["fact", ["edge", "a", "b"]]], stdlib, { database }));

await Effect.runPromise(run(["query", ["edge", "a", "?to"]], stdlib, { database }));
// => [{ to: "b" }]
```

Later runs see the database's relations by name, so they can query `edge` without declaring it again. Names you bind in the environment win over relations with the same name.

### Related

- [TypeScript API](https://lionlang.dev/docs.html#typescript-api) lists every export and option.
- [Add your own functions and algorithms](https://lionlang.dev/docs.html#extend-with-host-code) covers functions that work inside rules.
- [Names, scope, and environments](https://lionlang.dev/docs.html#names-and-scope) explains how lookups work.

---

## Run programs from the command line

URL: https://lionlang.dev/docs.html#use-the-cli
Section: How-to guides (How-to guide)

> Evaluate Lion files with the lion command, keep a logic database in a file between runs, and open the graph editor.

This guide shows how to use the `lion` command from `@lionlang/cli`.

### Install the command

```shell
bun add --dev @lionlang/cli
```

In a project, run it with `bun run lion`. Installed globally, it is just `lion`.

### Evaluate a file, inline expression, or standard input

Pass a JSON file, pass `--eval` (`-e`) for a quick one-liner, or pipe JSON into standard input (explicitly with `-` or implicitly when piped). Inject top-level JSON inputs with repeatable `--bind` (`-b`) or `--bind-file` flags, keeping exact numbers intact:

```shell
bun run lion add.json
bun run lion -e '["number/add", 1, 2]'
bun run lion -b tax=0.07 --bind-file order=order.json price.json
echo '["number/add", 1, 2]' | bun run lion -
```

If the input is not valid JSON, or the program fails, `lion` prints the error and exits with status 1.

### Check a program without running it

`lion check` reports malformed forms, misspelled names, wrong-arity calls, invalid `relation`/`query`/`invariant` options, unsafe rule heads or `find` templates, logic variables in ground facts, unreachable or non-exhaustive `match` cases, unreachable `cond` branches after `else`, duplicate lambda parameters, near-miss bare call heads, and Lion lints with JSON pointers. Pass `--database` or `--bind`/`--bind-file` to validate against external relations, schemas, and inputs read-only:

```shell
bun run lion check program.json
bun run lion check --database store.json -e '["query", ["edge", "a", "?to"]]'
bun run lion check --bind-file order=order.json price.json
```

### Keep and inspect a logic database in a file

Add `--database` with a path. Pass multiple step files to run them atomically in one invocation, pass `--read-only` (`-r`) for exploratory runs without touching disk, or run `lion inspect` to summarize a database's relations, schemas, invariants, and counts without reading the raw snapshot:

```shell
bun run lion 00-core.json 01-frame.json 02-facts.json --database store.json
bun run lion checks.json --database store.json
bun run lion --read-only --database store.json -e '["begin", ["fact", ["edge", "a", "z"]], ["find", "?x", ["path", "a", "?x"]]]'
bun run lion inspect store.json --derived
```

- A database file that does not exist yet starts empty.
- The file is a [snapshot](https://lionlang.dev/docs.html#save-and-load): an ordinary Lion program, one form and one fact per line, so it diffs well in version control.
- Read-only queries that make no committed changes do not rewrite an existing database file, so parallel queries stay fast and safe.
- If any program fails, for example because it would break an [invariant](https://lionlang.dev/docs.html#enforce-rules), the file is left as it was.
- Running the same setup again keeps one copy of each rule and invariant.

### Open the graph editor

```shell
bun run lion repl
bun run lion repl --host 0.0.0.0 --port 8080
```

The editor listens on `127.0.0.1:3000` unless you pass `--host` or `--port`. Open the address it prints, then open a `.json` program.

### Related

- [Command line](https://lionlang.dev/docs.html#cli) lists every command and flag.
- [Save and load a logic database](https://lionlang.dev/docs.html#save-and-load) shows the file format.

---

## Branch on a value's shape

URL: https://lionlang.dev/docs.html#branch-on-shape
Section: How-to guides (How-to guide)

> Choose what to do with a value based on its type or its structure, with match and cond.

This guide shows how to pick a branch based on what a value is. Use `match` when the choice depends on the value's type or structure, and `cond` when it depends on conditions you compute. The patterns of `match` are [schemas](https://lionlang.dev/docs.html#check-data).

### Branch on a value's type

Give `match` the value, then pairs of a schema and a function, then a fallback function. A predicate is a schema: the first one that returns `true` picks its function, which receives the value:

**Example: Match on type**

```json
["begin",
  ["define", "describe",
    ["lambda", ["value"],
      ["match", "value",
        ["value/number?", ["lambda", ["n"], "a number"]],
        ["value/string?", ["lambda", ["s"], ["string/concat", "a string: ", "s"]]],
        ["value/array?", ["lambda", ["xs"], "a list"]],
        ["lambda", ["other"], "something else"]]]],
  ["array/map", ["quote", [7, "hi", [1, 2], null]], "describe"]]
```

Result:

```json
["a number","a string: hi","a list","something else"]
```

### Branch on a record's structure

A record is a schema too. A record fits it when it has the same keys, with a value that fits the schema under each. A plain value fits a value equal to it, so a field can pick the branch. Records nest, and `schema/open` fits a record whatever other keys it has:

**Example: Match on structure**

```json
["begin",
  ["define", "route",
    ["lambda", ["message"],
      ["match", "message",
        [{"type": "order", "order": {"id": "value/number?"}},
         ["lambda", ["m"], ["object/get-path", "m", "order.id"]]],
        [{"type": ["schema/anyOf", "ping", "hello"]},
         ["lambda", ["m"], "pong"]],
        [["schema/open", {"type": "note"}],
         ["lambda", ["m"], ["object/get", "m", "text"]]],
        ["lambda", ["m"], "unknown message"]]]],
  ["array/map",
    ["quote", [
      {"type": "order", "order": {"id": 42}},
      {"type": "ping"},
      {"type": "note", "text": "call back", "from": "ada"},
      {"type": "order", "order": {"id": "x"}}]],
    "route"]]
```

Result:

```json
[42,"pong","call back","unknown message"]
```

A predicate that fails, or returns something other than `true`, counts as no match, so a pattern never crashes on data of the wrong type. A string in a pattern is a name first, as everywhere: `"order"` is the string unless something is bound to `order`, and `["quote", "order"]` is always the string.

### Branch on computed conditions

When the choice depends on comparisons, list condition and result pairs in `cond`, with an optional `else` at the end:

**Example: Cond**

```json
["begin",
  ["define", "grade",
    ["lambda", ["score"],
      ["cond",
        [["number/greaterThanOrEqualTo", "score", 90], "A"],
        [["number/greaterThanOrEqualTo", "score", 75], "B"],
        ["else", "C"]]]],
  ["array/map", ["array/make", 95, 80, 40], "grade"]]
```

Result:

```json
["A","B","C"]
```

Without an `else`, a `cond` with no matching condition returns `null`. Conditions use JavaScript truthiness: `false`, `null`, `0`, and `""` do not match, and every list and record does.

### Related

- [`match`](https://lionlang.dev/docs.html#form-match) and [`cond`](https://lionlang.dev/docs.html#form-cond) in the reference.
- [The `value` module](https://lionlang.dev/docs.html#module-value) lists the type predicates, and [the `schema` module](https://lionlang.dev/docs.html#module-schema) the functions that build schemas.
- [Check the shape of data](https://lionlang.dev/docs.html#check-data) shows what else a schema can do.

---

## Transform lists

URL: https://lionlang.dev/docs.html#transform-lists
Section: How-to guides (How-to guide)

> Make lists, map over them, filter them, flatten them, and fold them into a single value.

This guide shows how to work with lists using the `array` module and lambdas.

### Make a list

An array in a program is a call, so `[1, 2, 3]` on its own fails: `1` is not a function. Make a list with `array/make`, which evaluates its arguments, or with `quote`, which takes the list as written:

**Example: Make lists**

```json
{"made": ["array/make", 1, ["number/add", 1, 1], 3],
 "quoted": ["quote", [1, ["number/add", 1, 1], 3]],
 "range": ["array/range", 0, 5]}
```

Result:

```json
{
  "made": [1,2,3],
  "quoted": [1,["number/add",1,1],3],
  "range": [0,1,2,3,4]
}
```

### Change every item

Pass a list and a function to `array/map`:

**Example: Map**

```json
["array/map", ["array/range", 1, 6],
  ["lambda", ["n"], ["number/multiply", "n", "n"]]]
```

Result:

```json
[1,4,9,16,25]
```

### Keep some items

Pass a list and a predicate to `array/filter`. Its function gives `true` or `false`, as a condition does:

**Example: Filter**

```json
["array/filter", ["array/range", 1, 11],
  ["lambda", ["n"], ["number/greaterThan", "n", 6]]]
```

Result:

```json
[7,8,9,10]
```

### Reverse and sort

`array/reverse` puts items in reverse order. `array/sort` puts items in ascending canonical order, or stably sorts by a two-argument predicate that says when the first item comes before the second:

**Example: Reverse and sort**

```json
{"reversed": ["array/reverse", ["array/make", "a", "b", "c"]],
 "sorted": ["array/sort", ["array/make", 3, 1, 4, 1, 5]],
 "descending": ["array/sort", ["array/make", 3, 1, 4, 1, 5], "number/greaterThan"]}
```

Result:

```json
{
  "reversed": ["c","b","a"],
  "sorted": [1,1,3,4,5],
  "descending": [5,4,3,1,1]
}
```

### Combine items into one value

`array/reduce` takes a list, a starting value, and a function of the running value and the next item:

**Example: Reduce**

```json
["array/reduce", ["array/make", 3, 9, 4], 0,
  ["lambda", ["sum", "n"], ["number/add", "sum", "n"]]]
```

Result:

```json
16
```

For sums, counts, and other common totals, the [`aggregate` module](https://lionlang.dev/docs.html#module-aggregate) is shorter: `["aggregate/sum", list]`.

### Take lists apart

**Example: Take apart**

```json
{"first": ["array/head", ["array/make", "a", "b", "c"]],
 "rest": ["array/tail", ["array/make", "a", "b", "c"]],
 "length": ["array/length", ["array/make", "a", "b", "c"]],
 "hasB": ["array/includes?", ["array/make", "a", "b", "c"], "b"],
 "joined": ["array/concat", ["array/make", 1], ["array/make", 2, 3]]}
```

Result:

```json
{
  "first": "a",
  "rest": ["b","c"],
  "length": 3,
  "hasB": true,
  "joined": [1,2,3]
}
```

An empty list has no first item and no rest, so `array/head` and `array/tail` fail on one, as Scheme's `car` and `cdr` do. Ask for its length first, or use `array/slice`, which gives what part there is:

**Example: An empty list has no first item**

```json
["array/head", ["array/make"]]
```

Error:

```text
LogicError: "array/head" takes a list that is not empty as argument 1 but got [].
```

**Example: Taking the first item only when there is one**

```json
["begin",
  ["define", "first", ["lambda", ["items", "otherwise"],
    ["cond", [["number/equals?", ["array/length", "items"], 0], "otherwise"],
             ["else", ["array/head", "items"]]]]],
  {"of a list": ["first", ["array/make", "a", "b"], "none"],
   "of an empty one": ["first", ["array/make"], "none"],
   "a slice": ["array/slice", ["array/make"], 0, 1]}]
```

Result:

```json
{"of a list":"a","of an empty one":"none","a slice":[]}
```

### Related

- [The `array` module](https://lionlang.dev/docs.html#module-array) describes every list function.
- [`lambda`](https://lionlang.dev/docs.html#form-lambda) in the reference.

---

## Build and run code as data

URL: https://lionlang.dev/docs.html#code-as-data
Section: How-to guides (How-to guide)

> Hold a program as data, assemble one from parts, and run it with eval.

This guide shows how to treat Lion code as a value: keep it from running with `quote`, build it with ordinary functions, and run it with `eval`.

### Hold code without running it

`quote` returns its argument exactly as written:

**Example: Quote**

```json
["quote", ["number/add", 1, 2]]
```

Result:

```json
["number/add",1,2]
```

### Run code you hold

`eval` evaluates its argument, then evaluates the result as a program:

**Example: Eval**

```json
["begin",
  ["define", "formula", ["quote", ["number/multiply", "price", 2]]],
  ["define", "price", 21],
  ["eval", "formula"]]
```

Result:

```json
42
```

The code runs where `eval` is, so it sees the names defined there, including `price`, defined after the formula.

### Assemble a program from parts

A program is a list, so build it with list functions. Here a list of numbers becomes a chain of additions:

**Example: Build a program**

```json
["begin",
  ["define", "program",
    ["array/reduce", ["array/make", 2, 3, 4], 0,
      ["lambda", ["code", "n"],
        ["array/make", ["quote", "number/add"], "code", "n"]]]],
  {"program": "program", "result": ["eval", "program"]}]
```

Result:

```json
{
  "program": ["number/add",["number/add",["number/add",0,2],3],4],
  "result": 9
}
```

The name is quoted because `array/make` evaluates its arguments: unquoted, `"number/add"` would become the function itself, which is not JSON, so `eval` would refuse the program.

### Keep programs in records

Records evaluate their values, so quote programs you store as configuration and run the one you need:

**Example: Programs as config**

```json
["begin",
  ["define", "rules", {
    "short": ["quote", ["number/lessThan", ["string/length", "name"], 5]],
    "long": ["quote", ["number/greaterThan", ["string/length", "name"], 8]]}],
  ["define", "name", "Lion"],
  {"short": ["eval", ["object/get", "rules", "short"]],
   "long": ["eval", ["object/get", "rules", "long"]]}]
```

Result:

```json
{"short":true,"long":false}
```

### Related

- [`quote`](https://lionlang.dev/docs.html#form-quote) and [`eval`](https://lionlang.dev/docs.html#form-eval) in the reference.
- [Why programs are JSON](https://lionlang.dev/docs.html#why-json) explains why code and data share one shape.

---

## Query with conditions and computed values

URL: https://lionlang.dev/docs.html#query-with-conditions
Section: How-to guides (How-to guide)

> Narrow answers with comparisons, compute new values in rules and queries, choose between values, combine alternatives, and look inside lists.

This guide shows how to go beyond matching facts: filter answers with conditions, compute values, accept alternatives, and match items of a list.

### Filter answers with a condition

Call a function that answers `true` or `false` on a logic variable, and it becomes a filter. Combine goals with `and`:

**Example: Filter**

```json
["begin",
  ["relation", "order", ["id", "amount"]],
  ["fact", ["order", 1, 30], ["order", 2, 120], ["order", 3, 75]],
  ["query",
    ["and", ["order", "?id", "?amount"], ["number/greaterThan", "?amount", 50]],
    {"order": "id"}]]
```

Result:

```json
[{"id":2,"amount":120},{"id":3,"amount":75}]
```

A filter runs as soon as its variables are bound, so it can come before the goal that binds them. Filters that are ready together run in the order written. When some values would make a filter fail, put a guard before it:

**Example: Guard**

```json
["begin",
  ["relation", "reading", ["sensor", "value"]],
  ["fact", ["reading", "s1", 21], ["reading", "s2", "offline"], ["reading", "s3", 34]],
  ["query",
    ["and", ["reading", "?sensor", "?value"],
      ["value/number?", "?value"],
      ["number/greaterThan", "?value", 30]]]]
```

Result:

```json
[{"sensor":"s3","value":34}]
```

### Compute a value

Use `=` to bind a variable to a computed value:

**Example: Compute**

```json
["begin",
  ["relation", "order", ["id", "amount"]],
  ["fact", ["order", 1, 30], ["order", 2, 120]],
  ["query",
    ["and", ["order", "?id", "?amount"],
      ["=", "?withTax", ["number/multiply", "?amount", 1.25]]],
    {"order": "id"}]]
```

Result:

```json
[
  {"id":1,"amount":30,"withTax":37.5},
  {"id":2,"amount":120,"withTax":150}
]
```

In a rule, a computed value can also go straight into the head:

**Example: Compute in a rule**

```json
["begin",
  ["relation", "user", ["id", "first", "last"]],
  ["relation", "fullName", ["id", "name"]],
  ["fact", ["user", 1, "Ada", "Lovelace"], ["user", 2, "Alan", "Turing"]],
  ["rule", ["fullName", "?id", ["string/concat", ["string/concat", "?first", " "], "?last"]],
    ["user", "?id", "?first", "?last"]],
  ["query", ["fullName", "?id", "?name"], {"order": "id"}]]
```

Result:

```json
[{"id":1,"name":"Ada Lovelace"},{"id":2,"name":"Alan Turing"}]
```

### Choose between values

`cond`, `match`, and records work on logic variables too. Each waits until its variables are bound, then computes what it would with the values in place:

**Example: Choose**

```json
["begin",
  ["relation", "order", ["id", "amount"]],
  ["fact", ["order", 1, 30], ["order", 2, 120]],
  ["query",
    ["and", ["order", "?id", "?amount"],
      ["=", "?summary",
        {"size": ["cond", [["number/greaterThan", "?amount", 100], "large"], ["else", "small"]],
         "withTax": ["number/multiply", "?amount", 1.25]}]],
    {"order": "id"}]]
```

Result:

```json
[
  {"id":1,"amount":30,"summary":{"size":"small","withTax":37.5}},
  {"id":2,"amount":120,"summary":{"size":"large","withTax":150}}
]
```

Your own lambdas work the same way, including ones that branch or call themselves:

**Example: A lambda in a query**

```json
["begin",
  ["define", "factorial",
    ["lambda", ["n"],
      ["cond", [["number/lessThan", "n", 2], 1],
        ["else", ["number/multiply", "n", ["factorial", ["number/subtract", "n", 1]]]]]]],
  ["query",
    ["and", ["in", "?n", ["array/range", 1, 6]], ["=", "?f", ["factorial", "?n"]]]]]
```

Result:

```json
[
  {"n":1,"f":1},
  {"n":2,"f":2},
  {"n":3,"f":6},
  {"n":4,"f":24},
  {"n":5,"f":120}
]
```

### Leave answers out

`not` takes any goal: a relation call, a filter, or goals combined with `and` and `or`:

**Example: Not**

```json
["begin",
  ["relation", "order", ["id", "amount"]],
  ["relation", "refunded", ["id"]],
  ["fact", ["order", 1, 30], ["order", 2, 120], ["order", 3, 75]],
  ["fact", ["refunded", 3]],
  ["query",
    ["and", ["order", "?id", "?amount"],
      ["not", ["or", ["refunded", "?id"], ["number/lessThan", "?amount", 50]]]]]]
```

Result:

```json
[{"id":2,"amount":120}]
```

### Accept alternatives

`or` holds when any of its goals does:

**Example: Or**

```json
["begin",
  ["relation", "order", ["id", "status"]],
  ["fact", ["order", 1, "open"], ["order", 2, "paid"], ["order", 3, "held"]],
  ["query",
    ["or", ["order", "?id", "open"], ["order", "?id", "held"]],
    {"order": "id"}]]
```

Result:

```json
[{"id":1},{"id":3}]
```

### Match items of a list

When a fact holds a list, `in` binds a variable to each item:

**Example: In**

```json
["begin",
  ["relation", "post", ["id", "tags"]],
  ["fact",
    ["post", "p1", ["array/make", "lisp", "json"]],
    ["post", "p2", ["array/make", "json", "logic"]]],
  ["query",
    ["and", ["post", "?post", "?tags"], ["in", "json", "?tags"]],
    {"order": "post"}]]
```

Result:

```json
[
  {"post":"p1","tags":["lisp","json"]},
  {"post":"p2","tags":["json","logic"]}
]
```

With an unbound first argument, `in` binds it to each item; with a bound one, it tests membership, as above.

### Keep goals safe

Every variable in a filter, a computed value, or a `not` must be bound by a relation, `=`, `in`, or a [`schema/fits?` whose schema lists the values it allows](https://lionlang.dev/docs.html#take-data-apart) somewhere in the same goal. Otherwise there would be infinitely many answers, so Lion refuses the goal and names the variable:

**Example: Unsafe goal**

```json
["query", ["number/greaterThan", "?amount", 50]]
```

Error:

```text
LogicError: Unsafe goal ["number/greaterThan","?amount",50]: ?amount must first be bound by a relation, "=", "in", or "schema/fits?", or typed by a schema that says what kind its values are, such as value/integer?.
```

### Related

- [Logic forms](https://lionlang.dev/docs.html#logic-forms) describes `and`, `or`, `=`, and `in` exactly.
- [Logic database guarantees](https://lionlang.dev/docs.html#logic-guarantees) lists the safety rules.

---

## Use answers as values

URL: https://lionlang.dev/docs.html#ask-questions
Section: How-to guides (How-to guide)

> Ask the database from any expression: collect answers into a list with find, test a goal in cond, and use a relation as a predicate.

This guide shows how to use what the database knows inside ordinary expressions, in plain code and inside rules.

### Collect answers into a list

[`find`](https://lionlang.dev/docs.html#form-find) takes a template and a goal, and returns the template's value for every match of the goal, sorted:

**Example: Find**

```json
["begin",
  ["relation", "score", ["player", "points"]],
  ["fact", ["score", "ana", 12], ["score", "bo", 30], ["score", "cy", 30]],
  {"players": ["find", "?player", ["score", "?player", "?_"]],
   "by points": ["find", ["array/make", "?points", "?player"], ["score", "?player", "?points"]],
   "best": ["aggregate/max", ["find", "?points", ["score", "?_", "?points"]]]}]
```

Result:

```json
{
  "players": ["ana","bo","cy"],
  "by points": [[12,"ana"],[30,"bo"],[30,"cy"]],
  "best": 30
}
```

The result is a plain list, so every list function works on it. Where `query` returns one record per answer for you to read, `find` returns exactly the values you ask for.

### Test a goal

A goal is `true` when it has a match and `false` when it has none. Use it wherever a value is needed, such as a `cond` condition or a value of a record:

**Example: Goal as a value**

```json
["begin",
  ["relation", "member", ["name", "plan"]],
  ["relation", "blocked", ["name"]],
  ["fact", ["member", "ana", "pro"], ["member", "bo", "free"]],
  ["fact", ["blocked", "bo"]],
  ["define", "access",
    ["lambda", ["who"],
      ["cond",
        [["blocked", "who"], "none"],
        [["member", "who", "pro"], "full"],
        [["member", "who", "?_"], "limited"],
        ["else", "guest"]]]],
  {"ana": ["access", "ana"],
   "bo": ["access", "bo"],
   "zed": ["access", "zed"],
   "anyone blocked": ["blocked", "?_"]}]
```

Result:

```json
{"ana":"full","bo":"none","zed":"guest","anyone blocked":true}
```

A goal with a variable asks whether anything matches. Give a variable a name when the goal joins on it, as in `["and", ["member", "?m", "pro"], ["blocked", "?m"]]`.

### Use a relation as a predicate

A relation is a function that builds a goal, so it works as the predicate of `match` and of functions that take one:

**Example: Relation as a predicate**

```json
["begin",
  ["relation", "vowel", ["letter"]],
  ["fact", ["vowel", "a"], ["vowel", "e"], ["vowel", "i"], ["vowel", "o"], ["vowel", "u"]],
  {"flags": ["array/map", ["array/make", "l", "i", "o", "n"], "vowel"],
   "kind": ["match", "o",
     ["vowel", ["lambda", ["letter"], "a vowel"]],
     ["lambda", ["letter"], "a consonant"]]}]
```

Result:

```json
{"flags":[false,true,true,false],"kind":"a vowel"}
```

### Ask from inside a rule

In a rule or query the same expressions are asked once for each answer, with the answer's variables in place. A variable that only the question mentions, such as `?child` here, belongs to the question:

**Example: Ask in a rule**

```json
["begin",
  ["relation", "person", ["name"]],
  ["relation", "parent", ["parent", "child"]],
  ["relation", "profile", ["name", "summary"]],
  ["fact", ["person", "ada"], ["person", "ben"], ["person", "cy"]],
  ["fact", ["parent", "ada", "ben"], ["parent", "ada", "cy"]],
  ["rule",
    ["profile", "?p",
      {"children": ["find", "?child", ["parent", "?p", "?child"]],
       "kind": ["cond", [["parent", "?p", "?_"], "has children"], ["else", "no children"]]}],
    ["person", "?p"]],
  ["query", ["profile", "?name", "?summary"], {"order": "name"}]]
```

Result:

```json
[
  {
    "name": "ada",
    "summary": {"children":["ben","cy"],"kind":"has children"}
  },
  {"name":"ben","summary":{"children":[],"kind":"no children"}},
  {"name":"cy","summary":{"children":[],"kind":"no children"}}
]
```

A lambda that asks works in both places, because its body is asked wherever it runs:

**Example: A lambda that asks**

```json
["begin",
  ["relation", "person", ["name"]],
  ["relation", "parent", ["parent", "child"]],
  ["fact", ["person", "ada"], ["person", "ben"]],
  ["fact", ["parent", "ada", "ben"], ["parent", "ada", "cy"]],
  ["define", "children", ["lambda", ["p"], ["find", "?c", ["parent", "p", "?c"]]]],
  {"in plain code": ["children", "ada"],
   "in a query":
     ["query", ["and", ["person", "?p"], ["=", "?kids", ["children", "?p"]]], {"order": "p"}]}]
```

Result:

```json
{
  "in plain code": ["ben","cy"],
  "in a query": [{"p":"ada","kids":["ben","cy"]},{"p":"ben","kids":[]}]
}
```

### Keep a goal as a goal

`define`, `and`, `or`, `not`, and lambdas do not ask a goal: they keep it, so you can name goals and build bigger ones. Here the program's result is the goal itself:

**Example: Goals stay goals**

```json
["begin",
  ["relation", "member", ["name", "plan"]],
  ["define", "is-pro", ["member", "?who", "pro"]],
  ["and", "is-pro", ["not", ["member", "?who", "free"]]]]
```

Result:

```json
["and",["member","?who","pro"],["not",["member","?who","free"]]]
```

A goal is asked only where a value is needed. A record holds values, so it asks. To get a goal's truth on its own, give the goal to `value/identity`:

**Example: Ask a named goal**

```json
["begin",
  ["relation", "member", ["name", "plan"]],
  ["fact", ["member", "ana", "pro"]],
  ["define", "is-pro", ["member", "?who", "pro"]],
  {"in a record": "is-pro",
   "its truth": ["value/identity", "is-pro"],
   "its answers": ["query", "is-pro"]}]
```

Result:

```json
{
  "in a record": true,
  "its truth": true,
  "its answers": [{"who":"ana"}]
}
```

### Ask what would hold after a change

[`assuming`](https://lionlang.dev/docs.html#form-assuming) asks a question of the database as it would be after some `fact`, `retract`, and `rule` forms, and leaves the database as it is. In a rule it is asked for each answer, so a rule can try a change for every candidate. Here each shift that, given to one more person, would cover every day with two people:

**Example: What would hold**

```json
["begin",
  ["relation", "person", ["name"]],
  ["relation", "day", ["name"]],
  ["relation", "shift", ["person", "day"]],
  ["relation", "short", ["day"]],
  ["relation", "fixes", ["person", "day"]],
  ["fact", ["person", "ana"], ["person", "bo"], ["person", "cy"], ["day", "mon"], ["day", "tue"]],
  ["fact", ["shift", "ana", "mon"], ["shift", "bo", "mon"], ["shift", "ana", "tue"]],
  ["rule", ["short", "?d"],
    ["day", "?d"],
    ["number/lessThan", ["aggregate/count", ["find", "?p", ["shift", "?p", "?d"]]], 2]],
  ["rule", ["fixes", "?p", "?d"],
    ["person", "?p"], ["short", "?d"], ["not", ["shift", "?p", "?d"]],
    ["assuming", ["fact", ["shift", "?p", "?d"]], ["not", ["short", "?_"]]]],
  {"short now": ["find", "?d", ["short", "?d"]],
   "who would fix it": ["query", ["fixes", "?person", "?day"], {"order": "person"}]}]
```

Result:

```json
{
  "short now": ["tue"],
  "who would fix it": [{"person":"bo","day":"tue"},{"person":"cy","day":"tue"}]
}
```

### Related

- [Asking questions](https://lionlang.dev/docs.html#logic-asking) in the reference gives the exact rules.
- [Summarize groups of facts](https://lionlang.dev/docs.html#summarize-groups) uses `find` with aggregates.
- [Find what is missing](https://lionlang.dev/docs.html#find-missing) covers `not`.

---

## Sort, page, and check query answers

URL: https://lionlang.dev/docs.html#sort-and-page
Section: How-to guides (How-to guide)

> Order answers by one or more variables, take a page of them, and make a query fail when it finds too few or too many.

This guide shows how to use query options, the record after a query's goal.

### Sort answers

Give `"order"` a variable name, or a list of them to break ties. A leading `-` sorts that variable from largest to smallest:

**Example: Order**

```json
["begin",
  ["relation", "score", ["player", "points"]],
  ["fact", ["score", "ana", 12], ["score", "bo", 30], ["score", "cy", 30], ["score", "dee", 7]],
  ["query", ["score", "?player", "?points"], {"order": ["-points", "player"]}]]
```

Result:

```json
[
  {"player":"bo","points":30},
  {"player":"cy","points":30},
  {"player":"ana","points":12},
  {"player":"dee","points":7}
]
```

### Take a page

`"offset"` skips answers and `"limit"` caps how many come back. Sort first, so pages are stable:

**Example: Page**

```json
["begin",
  ["relation", "score", ["player", "points"]],
  ["fact", ["score", "ana", 12], ["score", "bo", 30], ["score", "cy", 30], ["score", "dee", 7]],
  ["query", ["score", "?player", "?points"], {"order": "-points", "offset": 1, "limit": 2}]]
```

Result:

```json
[{"player":"cy","points":30},{"player":"ana","points":12}]
```

### Fail when there are no answers, or some

`"assert": "some"` makes the query fail when it has no answers, and `"assert": "none"` when it has any. Use it to stop a program early when data is not as expected:

**Example: Assert**

```json
["begin",
  ["relation", "score", ["player", "points"]],
  ["fact", ["score", "ana", 12]],
  ["query", ["score", "?player", "?points"], {"assert": "none"}]]
```

Error:

```text
LogicError: The query expected no answers but found 1, such as {"player":"ana","points":12}: ["score","?player","?points"].
```

The assertion sees every answer, before `offset` and `limit`. To keep a check like this in force after every change, use an [invariant](https://lionlang.dev/docs.html#enforce-rules).

### Related

- [Query options](https://lionlang.dev/docs.html#query-options) describes each option and the order of values across types.

---

## Follow relationships of any length

URL: https://lionlang.dev/docs.html#recursive-relations
Section: How-to guides (How-to guide)

> Derive paths, reachability, and hierarchies with recursive rules, and write them so queries stay fast.

This guide shows how to follow a relationship through any number of steps, such as routes through a network or managers up an org chart.

### Write the two rules
