## Prove that every command keeps a rule

URL: https://lionlang.dev/docs.html#prove-commands
Section: How-to guides (How-to guide)

> Prove for every state and every command that a step keeps a rule, see a state that breaks the proof, find the rules a proof needs, check a proof's certificate yourself, and ask whether one schema includes another.

This guide shows how to prove that a model keeps a rule: not for the runs a search tried, but for every state the rule allows and every command, which is the step of a proof by induction. A schema types the state and the command, and [the solver](https://lionlang.dev/docs.html#solve-for-values) works out every value they can take.

### Prove that a command keeps a rule

An account has a balance and an overdraft limit, and a withdrawal that would go past the limit is refused. A rule is kept when no state the rule allows, and no command, leads to a state that breaks it. Ask whether such a state exists, under `not`: `[{}]` is the proof, for every account and every command, and `[]` says some state and command break the rule:

**Example: A rule every command keeps**

```json
["begin",
  ["schema", "Account", {"balance": "value/integer?", "limit": "value/integer?"}],
  ["schema", "Amount", ["schema/allOf", "value/integer?", ["lambda", ["n"], ["number/greaterThan", "n", 0]]]],
  ["schema", "Command", ["schema/anyOf", {"deposit": "Amount"}, {"withdraw": "Amount"}]],
  ["define", "step", ["lambda", ["a", "c"], ["cond", [["object/has?", "c", "deposit"], {"balance": ["number/add", ["object/get", "a", "balance"], ["object/get", "c", "deposit"]], "limit": ["object/get", "a", "limit"]}], [["number/lessThan", ["number/add", ["object/get", "a", "balance"], ["object/get", "a", "limit"]], ["object/get", "c", "withdraw"]], "a"], ["else", {"balance": ["number/subtract", ["object/get", "a", "balance"], ["object/get", "c", "withdraw"]], "limit": ["object/get", "a", "limit"]}]]]],
  ["define", "within limit", ["lambda", ["a"], ["number/greaterThanOrEqualTo", ["number/add", ["object/get", "a", "balance"], ["object/get", "a", "limit"]], 0]]],
  ["define", "limit not negative", ["lambda", ["a"], ["number/greaterThanOrEqualTo", ["object/get", "a", "limit"], 0]]],
  ["define", "not overdrawn", ["lambda", ["a"], ["number/greaterThanOrEqualTo", ["object/get", "a", "balance"], 0]]],
  ["define", "keeps", ["lambda", ["rule"], ["query", ["not", ["exists", ["?a", "?c"], ["and", ["schema/fits?", "?a", "Account"], ["rule", "?a"], ["schema/fits?", "?c", "Command"], ["not", ["rule", ["step", "?a", "?c"]]]]]]]]],
  {"within limit": ["keeps", "within limit"], "not overdrawn": ["keeps", "not overdrawn"]}]
```

Result:

```json
{"within limit":[{}],"not overdrawn":[]}
```

Staying within the limit is kept; never being overdrawn is not, since an account with a limit may go below 0.

### See a state that breaks the proof

A rule that holds when the state that breaks the proof exists, and `why`, give that state and command. The state may never be reached from where the model starts: then the rule needs another one beside it that rules the state out.

**Example: A state that breaks the proof**

```json
["begin",
  ["schema", "Account", {"balance": "value/integer?", "limit": "value/integer?"}],
  ["schema", "Amount", ["schema/allOf", "value/integer?", ["lambda", ["n"], ["number/greaterThan", "n", 0]]]],
  ["schema", "Command", ["schema/anyOf", {"deposit": "Amount"}, {"withdraw": "Amount"}]],
  ["define", "step", ["lambda", ["a", "c"], ["cond", [["object/has?", "c", "deposit"], {"balance": ["number/add", ["object/get", "a", "balance"], ["object/get", "c", "deposit"]], "limit": ["object/get", "a", "limit"]}], [["number/lessThan", ["number/add", ["object/get", "a", "balance"], ["object/get", "a", "limit"]], ["object/get", "c", "withdraw"]], "a"], ["else", {"balance": ["number/subtract", ["object/get", "a", "balance"], ["object/get", "c", "withdraw"]], "limit": ["object/get", "a", "limit"]}]]]],
  ["define", "within limit", ["lambda", ["a"], ["number/greaterThanOrEqualTo", ["number/add", ["object/get", "a", "balance"], ["object/get", "a", "limit"]], 0]]],
  ["define", "limit not negative", ["lambda", ["a"], ["number/greaterThanOrEqualTo", ["object/get", "a", "limit"], 0]]],
  ["define", "not overdrawn", ["lambda", ["a"], ["number/greaterThanOrEqualTo", ["object/get", "a", "balance"], 0]]],
  ["define", "keeps", ["lambda", ["rule"], ["query", ["not", ["exists", ["?a", "?c"], ["and", ["schema/fits?", "?a", "Account"], ["rule", "?a"], ["schema/fits?", "?c", "Command"], ["not", ["rule", ["step", "?a", "?c"]]]]]]]]],
  ["relation", "breaks", ["rule"]],
  ["rule", ["breaks", ["quote", "not overdrawn"]], ["schema/fits?", "?a", "Account"], ["not overdrawn", "?a"], ["schema/fits?", "?c", "Command"], ["not", ["not overdrawn", ["step", "?a", "?c"]]]],
  ["object/get", ["array/head", ["object/get", ["why", ["breaks", ["quote", "not overdrawn"]]], "because"]], "example"]]
```

Result:

```json
{"?a":{"balance":0,"limit":1},"?c":{"withdraw":1}}
```

### Notice a proof that holds of no state

A proof that a rule is kept asks whether any state the rule allows, and any command, break it. When the rule allows no state at all, no state breaks it, and the proof holds of nothing. Write the proof as a rule, and `why` says which goals contradict each other, and `"vacuous": true` when they leave out the goal the proof denies:

**Example: A proof that holds of no state**

```json
["begin",
  ["schema", "Account", {"balance": "value/integer?", "limit": "value/integer?"}],
  ["schema", "Amount", ["schema/allOf", "value/integer?", ["lambda", ["n"], ["number/greaterThan", "n", 0]]]],
  ["schema", "Command", ["schema/anyOf", {"deposit": "Amount"}, {"withdraw": "Amount"}]],
  ["define", "step", ["lambda", ["a", "c"], ["cond", [["object/has?", "c", "deposit"], {"balance": ["number/add", ["object/get", "a", "balance"], ["object/get", "c", "deposit"]], "limit": ["object/get", "a", "limit"]}], ["else", {"balance": ["number/subtract", ["object/get", "a", "balance"], ["object/get", "c", "withdraw"]], "limit": ["object/get", "a", "limit"]}]]]],
  ["define", "never and always overdrawn", ["lambda", ["a"], ["boolean/and", ["number/greaterThanOrEqualTo", ["object/get", "a", "balance"], 0], ["number/lessThan", ["object/get", "a", "balance"], 0]]]],
  ["relation", "kept", ["rule"]],
  ["rule", ["kept", ["quote", "never and always overdrawn"]],
    ["not", ["exists", ["?a", "?c"], ["and", ["schema/fits?", "?a", "Account"], ["never and always overdrawn", "?a"], ["schema/fits?", "?c", "Command"], ["not", ["never and always overdrawn", ["step", "?a", "?c"]]]]]]],
  ["define", "told", ["array/head", ["object/get", ["why", ["kept", ["quote", "never and always overdrawn"]]], "because"]]],
  {"vacuous": ["object/get", "told", "vacuous"], "contradicting": ["object/get", "told", "contradicting"]}]
```

Result:

```json
{
  "vacuous": true,
  "contradicting": [
    [
      "boolean/and",
      [
        "number/greaterThanOrEqualTo",
        ["object/get","?a","balance"],
        0
      ],
      ["number/lessThan",["object/get","?a","balance"],0]
    ]
  ]
}
```

The withdrawals have no limit here, so the proof that the account is never overdrawn and always overdrawn holds; `why` shows it holds only because no account meets the rule.

### Find the rules a proof needs

A rule may be kept only together with others. Houdini's way finds the largest set of candidate rules that keeps itself: drop each candidate that some state the others allow, and some command, break, and ask again, until none is dropped. In Lion it is a few lines over the same question:

**Example: The rules a proof needs**

```json
["begin",
  ["schema", "Account", {"balance": "value/integer?", "limit": "value/integer?"}],
  ["schema", "Amount", ["schema/allOf", "value/integer?", ["lambda", ["n"], ["number/greaterThan", "n", 0]]]],
  ["schema", "Command", ["schema/anyOf", {"deposit": "Amount"}, {"withdraw": "Amount"}]],
  ["define", "step", ["lambda", ["a", "c"], ["cond", [["object/has?", "c", "deposit"], {"balance": ["number/add", ["object/get", "a", "balance"], ["object/get", "c", "deposit"]], "limit": ["object/get", "a", "limit"]}], [["number/lessThan", ["number/add", ["object/get", "a", "balance"], ["object/get", "a", "limit"]], ["object/get", "c", "withdraw"]], "a"], ["else", {"balance": ["number/subtract", ["object/get", "a", "balance"], ["object/get", "c", "withdraw"]], "limit": ["object/get", "a", "limit"]}]]]],
  ["define", "within limit", ["lambda", ["a"], ["number/greaterThanOrEqualTo", ["number/add", ["object/get", "a", "balance"], ["object/get", "a", "limit"]], 0]]],
  ["define", "limit not negative", ["lambda", ["a"], ["number/greaterThanOrEqualTo", ["object/get", "a", "limit"], 0]]],
  ["define", "not overdrawn", ["lambda", ["a"], ["number/greaterThanOrEqualTo", ["object/get", "a", "balance"], 0]]],
  ["define", "keeps", ["lambda", ["rule"], ["query", ["not", ["exists", ["?a", "?c"], ["and", ["schema/fits?", "?a", "Account"], ["rule", "?a"], ["schema/fits?", "?c", "Command"], ["not", ["rule", ["step", "?a", "?c"]]]]]]]]],
  ["define", "candidates", {"within limit": "within limit", "limit not negative": "limit not negative", "not overdrawn": "not overdrawn"}],
  ["define", "holds all", ["lambda", ["names", "a"], ["array/every?", "names", ["lambda", ["n"], [["object/get", "candidates", "n"], "a"]]]]],
  ["define", "kept", ["lambda", ["names", "name"], ["not", ["exists", ["?a", "?c"], ["and", ["schema/fits?", "?a", "Account"], ["holds all", "names", "?a"], ["schema/fits?", "?c", "Command"], ["not", [["object/get", "candidates", "name"], ["step", "?a", "?c"]]]]]]]],
  ["define", "houdini", ["lambda", ["names"], ["begin", ["define", "survivors", ["find", "?n", ["and", ["in", "?n", "names"], ["kept", "names", "?n"]]]], ["cond", [["number/equals?", ["array/length", "survivors"], ["array/length", "names"]], "names"], ["else", ["houdini", "survivors"]]]]]],
  ["houdini", ["quote", ["within limit", "limit not negative", "not overdrawn"]]]]
```

Result:

```json
["limit not negative","within limit"]
```

### Check a proof yourself

Where a step of the solver stopped a rule, `why` shows a `certificate` for each case the solver split the goals into: the constraints, as whole-number sums compared with 0, and steps that each add earlier lines, each multiplied by a whole number, and over whole numbers may tighten the sum, dividing it by the greatest common divisor of its coefficients and rounding its constant down. The last line has no variables and is false, so the constraints have no solution. Checking it takes only arithmetic, so a small program can, without trusting the solver. Here one in Lion checks the certificate `why` gives:

**Example: A proof checked by a small program**

```json
["begin",
  ["relation", "limit", ["n"]],
  ["relation", "room", ["n"]],
  ["fact", ["limit", 3]],
  ["rule", ["room", "?n"], ["limit", "?n"], ["schema/fits?", "?x", "value/integer?"], ["number/greaterThan", "?x", 2], ["number/lessThan", "?x", "?n"]],
  ["define", "gcd", ["lambda", ["a", "b"], ["cond", [["number/equals?", "b", 0], ["number/absolute", "a"]], ["else", ["gcd", "b", ["number/remainder", "a", "b"]]]]]],
  ["define", "add line", ["lambda", ["total", "line", "times"], {"sum": ["array/reduce", ["object/keys", ["object/get", "line", "sum"]], ["object/get", "total", "sum"], ["lambda", ["acc", "name"], ["object/set", "acc", "name", ["number/add", ["cond", [["array/includes?", ["object/keys", "acc"], "name"], ["object/get", "acc", "name"]], ["else", 0]], ["number/multiply", "times", ["object/get", ["object/get", "line", "sum"], "name"]]]]]], "constant": ["number/add", ["object/get", "total", "constant"], ["number/multiply", "times", ["object/get", "line", "constant"]]], "relation": ["cond", [["string/equals?", ["object/get", "line", ["quote", "relation"]], ["quote", "="]], ["object/get", "total", ["quote", "relation"]]], [["boolean/or", ["string/equals?", ["object/get", "line", ["quote", "relation"]], ">"], ["string/equals?", ["object/get", "total", ["quote", "relation"]], ">"]], ">"], ["else", ">="]]}]],
  ["define", "tighten", ["lambda", ["line"], ["begin", ["define", "strict?", ["string/equals?", ["object/get", "line", ["quote", "relation"]], ">"]], ["define", "lowered", ["number/subtract", ["object/get", "line", "constant"], ["cond", ["strict?", 1], ["else", 0]]]], ["define", "divisor", ["array/reduce", ["object/values", ["object/get", "line", "sum"]], 0, "gcd"]], ["cond", [["number/lessThanOrEqualTo", "divisor", 1], {"sum": ["object/get", "line", "sum"], "constant": "lowered", "relation": ["cond", ["strict?", ">="], ["else", ["object/get", "line", ["quote", "relation"]]]]}], ["else", {"sum": ["array/reduce", ["object/keys", ["object/get", "line", "sum"]], {}, ["lambda", ["acc", "name"], ["object/set", "acc", "name", ["number/divide", ["object/get", ["object/get", "line", "sum"], "name"], "divisor"]]]], "constant": ["cond", [["string/equals?", ["object/get", "line", ["quote", "relation"]], ["quote", "="]], ["number/divide", "lowered", "divisor"]], ["else", ["number/floor", ["number/divide", "lowered", "divisor"]]]], "relation": ["cond", ["strict?", ">="], ["else", ["object/get", "line", ["quote", "relation"]]]]}]]]]],
  ["define", "false?", ["lambda", ["line"], ["boolean/and", ["array/every?", ["object/values", ["object/get", "line", "sum"]], ["lambda", ["k"], ["number/equals?", "k", 0]]], ["cond", [["string/equals?", ["object/get", "line", ["quote", "relation"]], ">="], ["number/lessThan", ["object/get", "line", "constant"], 0]], [["string/equals?", ["object/get", "line", ["quote", "relation"]], ">"], ["number/lessThanOrEqualTo", ["object/get", "line", "constant"], 0]], ["else", ["boolean/not", ["number/equals?", ["object/get", "line", "constant"], 0]]]]]]],
  ["define", "checks", ["lambda", ["given"], ["false?", ["array/head", ["array/slice", ["array/reduce", ["object/get", "given", "steps"], ["object/get", "given", "constraints"], ["lambda", ["lines", "step"], ["begin", ["define", "made", ["array/reduce", ["object/get", "step", "from"], {"sum": {}, "constant": 0, "relation": ["quote", "="]}, ["lambda", ["total", "use"], ["add line", "total", ["array/head", ["array/slice", "lines", ["array/head", "use"]]], ["array/head", ["array/tail", "use"]]]]]], ["array/concat", "lines", ["array/make", ["cond", [["object/get", "step", "tightened"], ["tighten", "made"]], ["else", "made"]]]]]]], -1]]]]],
  ["define", "proof", ["object/get", ["object/get", ["array/head", ["object/get", ["why", ["room", 3]], "because"]], "but"], "certificate"]],
  {"certificate": "proof", "every case checks": ["array/every?", "proof", "checks"]}]
```

Result:

```json
{
  "certificate": [
    {
      "constraints": [
        {"constant":-2,"relation":">","sum":{"x":1}},
        {"constant":3,"relation":">","sum":{"x":-1}}
      ],
      "steps": [
        {"from":[[0,1]],"tightened":true},
        {"from":[[1,1]],"tightened":true},
        {"from":[[2,1],[3,1]],"tightened":true}
      ]
    }
  ],
  "every case checks": true
}
```

A case that needs the Omega test's dark and grey shadows over whole numbers receives a binary integer split tree (`kind: "split"`) whose leaves are linear certificates. Lion also provides [`proof/valid?`](https://lionlang.dev/docs.html#module-proof), a small trusted kernel that checks linear certificates, split trees, induction proofs, lemmas, and `why` derivations with plain arithmetic and without invoking the solver.

### Prove properties by induction

For universal questions (`["not", ["exists", ...]]`) over recursive named schemas, unbounded lists (`schema/arrayOf`), or lower-bounded integers, the solver proves by structural or numeric induction whenever the recursive functions involved are pure, strictly decrease on a structural sub-part or lower-bounded integer measure, and return a uniform sort. Products of unknowns are tracked as exact polynomials so matching nonlinear terms cancel in induction steps:

**Example: Structural and numeric induction**

```json
["begin",
  ["schema", "PosInt", ["schema/allOf", "value/integer?", ["lambda", ["n"], ["number/greaterThanOrEqualTo", "n", 1]]]],
  ["schema", "Tree", ["schema/anyOf", {"leaf": "PosInt"}, {"node": {"left": "Tree", "right": "Tree", "val": "PosInt"}}]],
  ["define", "tree-sum", ["lambda", ["t"],
    ["cond",
      [["object/has?", "t", "leaf"], ["object/get", "t", "leaf"]],
      ["else", ["number/add",
        ["object/get", ["object/get", "t", "node"], "val"],
        ["tree-sum", ["object/get", ["object/get", "t", "node"], "left"]],
        ["tree-sum", ["object/get", ["object/get", "t", "node"], "right"]]]]]]],
  ["define", "sum-odd", ["lambda", ["n"],
    ["cond",
      [["number/lessThanOrEqualTo", "n", 0], 0],
      ["else", ["number/add", ["sum-odd", ["number/subtract", "n", 1]], ["number/subtract", ["number/multiply", 2, "n"], 1]]]]]],
  {"every tree sum is positive": ["query", ["not", ["exists", ["?t"],
     ["and", ["schema/fits?", "?t", "Tree"], ["number/lessThan", ["tree-sum", "?t"], 1]]]]],
   "sum of first n odd numbers is n^2": ["query", ["not", ["exists", ["?n"],
     ["and", ["schema/fits?", "?n", "value/integer?"],
             ["number/greaterThanOrEqualTo", "?n", 0],
             ["not", ["number/equals?", ["sum-odd", "?n"], ["number/multiply", "?n", "?n"]]]]]]]}]
```

Result:

```json
{
  "every tree sum is positive": [{}],
  "sum of first n odd numbers is n^2": [{}]
}
```

### Prove properties of rules by rule induction

`proof/rules` proves universally over all databases whose base relations fit their declared schemas that every row derived by a relation (or a record of mutually recursive relations) fits a target schema, returning a proof value checkable by `proof/valid?`:

**Example: Rule induction over a recursive relation**

```json
["begin",
  ["schema", "PosCost", ["schema/allOf", "value/integer?", ["lambda", ["n"], ["number/greaterThanOrEqualTo", "n", 1]]]],
  ["schema", "PosEdge", {"from": "value/string?", "to": "value/string?", "cost": "PosCost"}],
  ["relation", "edge", ["from", "to", "cost"], {"schema": "PosEdge"}],
  ["relation", "path", ["from", "to", "cost"]],
  ["rule", ["path", "?a", "?b", ["aggregate/min", "?c"]], ["edge", "?a", "?b", "?c"]],
  ["rule", ["path", "?a", "?c", ["aggregate/min", ["number/add", "?c1", "?c2"]]], ["edge", "?a", "?b", "?c1"], ["path", "?b", "?c", "?c2"]],
  ["define", "p", ["proof/rules", "path", "PosEdge"]],
  {"proved": ["object/get", "p", "proved"], "kernel valid": ["proof/valid?", "p"]}]
```

Result:

```json
{"proved":true,"kernel valid":true}
```

### Prove goals, synthesize counterexamples, and compute exact bounds

`proof/prove` decides a universal or empirical goal in one call, returning a kernel-checked certificate or a concrete `counterexample` witness when a universal claim fails. `proof/bounds` computes exact tight `min` and `max` bounds across continuous linear, integer and mixed-integer linear, linear-fractional ratio (continuous Charnes-Cooper and integer Dinkelbach), bilinear/quadratic, and symbolic `time/` constraints, with endpoint witnesses and kernel-valid `minProof` / `maxProof` certificates — checkable directly and bound to a threshold claim with 2-argument `proof/valid?`:

**Example: Exact ratio bounds, bilinear extrema, and claim-bound verification**

```json
["begin",
  ["define", "rel", ["proof/bounds",
    ["number/divide", "?s", ["number/add", "?s", "?f"]],
    ["and",
      ["schema/fits?", "?s", "value/integer?"], ["schema/fits?", "?f", "value/integer?"],
      ["number/greaterThanOrEqualTo", "?s", ["number/add", ["number/multiply", 2, "?f"], 21]],
      ["number/lessThanOrEqualTo", ["number/add", "?s", "?f"], 43],
      ["number/greaterThanOrEqualTo", "?f", 6], ["number/lessThanOrEqualTo", "?f", 10],
      ["number/lessThanOrEqualTo", "?s", 37]]]],
  ["define", "rev", ["proof/bounds",
    ["number/multiply", "?n", "?p"],
    ["and",
      ["schema/fits?", "?n", "value/integer?"], ["schema/fits?", "?p", "value/number?"],
      ["number/greaterThanOrEqualTo", "?n", 4], ["number/lessThanOrEqualTo", "?n", 14],
      ["number/greaterThanOrEqualTo", "?p", 12], ["number/lessThanOrEqualTo", "?p", 22],
      ["number/lessThanOrEqualTo", ["number/add", "?p", ["number/multiply", 2, "?n"]], 36]]]],
  {"minReliabilityPct": ["number/round", ["number/multiply", 100, ["object/get", "rel", "min"]], 2],
   "maxReliabilityPct": ["number/round", ["number/multiply", 100, ["object/get", "rel", "max"]], 2],
   "clears83Pct": ["proof/valid?", "rel", {"atLeast": 0.83}],
   "minRevenue": ["object/get", "rev", "min"],
   "maxRevenue": ["object/get", "rev", "max"],
   "maxRevWitness": ["object/get", "rev", "witnessMax"]}]
```

Result:

```json
{
  "minReliabilityPct": 83.33,
  "maxReliabilityPct": 86.05,
  "clears83Pct": true,
  "minRevenue": 48,
  "maxRevenue": 162,
  "maxRevWitness": {"?n":9,"?p":18}
}
```

### Measure epistemic fragility with `proof/sensitivity`

`proof/sensitivity` checks every derivation of a ground conclusion in the database and reports whether it is `resilient` to any single-fact retraction, which base facts are `critical` (single points of failure), and the smallest joint retractions (`minimalCuts`) that break it:

**Example: All-derivations fragility and minimal cut sets**

```json
["begin",
  ["relation", "edge", ["from", "to"]],
  ["relation", "reach", ["from", "to"]],
  ["fact", ["edge", "a", "b"], ["edge", "b", "d"], ["edge", "a", "c"], ["edge", "c", "d"]],
  ["rule", ["reach", "?x", "?y"], ["edge", "?x", "?y"]],
  ["rule", ["reach", "?x", "?z"], ["reach", "?x", "?y"], ["edge", "?y", "?z"]],
  ["proof/sensitivity", ["reach", "a", "d"]]]
```

Result:

```json
{
  "critical": [],
  "holds": true,
  "minCutSize": 2,
  "minimalCuts": [
    [["edge","a","b"],["edge","a","c"]],
    [["edge","a","b"],["edge","c","d"]],
    [["edge","a","c"],["edge","b","d"]],
    [["edge","b","d"],["edge","c","d"]]
  ],
  "redundant": [["edge","a","b"],["edge","b","d"]],
  "resilient": true
}
```

### Ask whether one schema includes another

`schema/includes?` says whether every value one schema allows fits another, exactly: by listing the first schema's values when it can list them, and by the solver otherwise — across value kinds, open records and lists, unbounded collections, and recursive or mutually recursive named schemas (including uninhabited recursive schemas). It refuses, and says why, only when neither can decide an arbitrary predicate:

**Example: One schema in another**

```json
["begin",
  ["schema", "PosInt", ["schema/allOf", "value/integer?", ["lambda", ["n"], ["number/greaterThan", "n", 0]]],
    "NonNeg", ["schema/allOf", "value/integer?", ["lambda", ["n"], ["number/greaterThanOrEqualTo", "n", 0]]],
    "PosTree", ["schema/anyOf", {"leaf": "PosInt"}, {"node": {"left": "PosTree", "right": "PosTree"}}],
    "NonNegTree", ["schema/anyOf", {"leaf": "NonNeg"}, {"node": {"left": "NonNegTree", "right": "NonNegTree"}}]],
  {"whole numbers are numbers": ["schema/includes?", "value/integer?", "value/number?"],
   "not every number is whole": ["schema/includes?", "value/number?", "value/integer?"],
   "strings are not numbers": ["schema/includes?", "value/string?", "value/number?"],
   "open record in exact record": ["schema/includes?", ["schema/open", {"x": "value/integer?"}], {"x": "value/integer?"}],
   "positive amounts are not negative": ["schema/includes?", "PosInt", "NonNeg"],
   "and not the other way": ["schema/includes?", "NonNeg", "PosInt"],
   "positive trees are non-negative trees": ["schema/includes?", "PosTree", "NonNegTree"],
   "lists are empty or non-empty": ["schema/includes?", ["schema/arrayOf", "value/integer?"], ["schema/anyOf", ["quote", []], ["schema/open", ["array/make", "value/integer?"], ["schema/arrayOf", "value/integer?"]]]],
   "a listed schema": ["schema/includes?", ["schema/anyOf", 1, 2], ["schema/anyOf", 1, 2, 3]]}]
```

Result:

```json
{
  "whole numbers are numbers": true,
  "not every number is whole": false,
  "strings are not numbers": false,
  "open record in exact record": false,
  "positive amounts are not negative": true,
  "and not the other way": false,
  "positive trees are non-negative trees": true,
  "lists are empty or non-empty": true,
  "a listed schema": true
}
```

### Related

- [Solve for values and prove rules](https://lionlang.dev/docs.html#solve-for-values): what the solver decides.
- [Check every run of commands](https://lionlang.dev/docs.html#check-every-run): rules over the states of every run up to a length.

---

## Check the shape of data

URL: https://lionlang.dev/docs.html#check-data
Section: How-to guides (How-to guide)

> Say what a value must be with a schema, find where data does not fit, and have a relation refuse rows that do not.

This guide shows how to check data against a schema. A schema says what a value must be, and Lion has one rule for what fits one: a function is a predicate, a record or list fits part by part, and any other value fits a value equal to it.

### Describe a record

Write the record you expect, with a schema in place of each value. `schema/fits?` asks whether a value fits, and `schema/problems` lists every place where it does not:

**Example: A record**

```json
["begin",
  ["define", "Order",
    {"id": "value/integer?",
     "status": ["schema/anyOf", "open", "shipped"],
     "note": ["schema/optional", "value/string?"]}],
  ["define", "incoming", ["quote", {"id": "7", "status": "opne"}]],
  {"fits": ["schema/fits?", "incoming", "Order"],
   "problems": ["schema/problems", "incoming", "Order"]}]
```

Result:

```json
{
  "fits": false,
  "problems": [
    {"path":["id"],"expected":"value/integer?","found":"7"},
    {
      "path": ["status"],
      "expected": ["schema/anyOf","open","shipped"],
      "found": "opne"
    }
  ]
}
```

Each problem has the `path` to the part that does not fit, the schema that was `expected` there, and the value that was `found`. A record schema fits a record with the same keys, so a key it does not name is a problem too, with only what was `found`. Wrap the record in `schema/open` to allow other keys.

### Allow keys you do not name

A record schema says every key the record has. To check some keys and let the rest be, wrap the record in `schema/open`. To let one key be left out, give it `schema/optional`:

**Example: Other keys**

```json
["begin",
  ["define", "incoming", ["quote", {"id": 7, "status": "open", "rush": true}]],
  {"exact": ["schema/problems", "incoming",
     {"id": "value/integer?", "status": "value/string?"}],
   "open": ["schema/fits?", "incoming",
     ["schema/open", {"id": "value/integer?", "status": "value/string?"}]],
   "optional": ["schema/fits?", "incoming",
     {"id": "value/integer?", "status": "value/string?",
      "rush": ["schema/optional", "value/boolean?"],
      "note": ["schema/optional", "value/string?"]}]}]
```

Result:

```json
{
  "exact": [{"path":["rush"],"found":true}],
  "open": true,
  "optional": true
}
```

### Build one schema from two

A record schema is exact, so `schema/allOf` of two record schemas with different keys fits nothing: each refuses the other's keys. Give `schema/open` the second as the schema of the rest instead. The keys the first names are checked against it, and the record of the other keys against the second, so the two make one exact schema. Any schema can check the rest, such as `schema/recordOf` for keys you cannot name in advance:

**Example: Composed schemas**

```json
["begin",
  ["schema", "Entity", {"id": "value/integer?", "created": "value/string?"}],
  ["schema", "Line", {"sku": "value/string?", "qty": "value/integer?"}],
  ["schema", "Stock", ["schema/open", "Entity", "Line"]],
  ["define", "incoming", ["quote", {"id": 4, "created": "2026-11-18", "sku": "a1", "qty": 2, "rush": true}]],
  {"allOf": ["schema/fits?", "incoming", ["schema/allOf", "Entity", "Line"]],
   "composed": ["schema/problems", "incoming", "Stock"],
   "string extras": ["schema/fits?", "incoming",
     ["schema/open", "Entity", ["schema/recordOf", "value/string?"]]]}]
```

Result:

```json
{
  "allOf": false,
  "composed": [{"path":["rush"],"found":true}],
  "string extras": false
}
```

### Check lists and plain values

A list of schemas fits a list of the same length, item by item, which suits a pair or a triple. `schema/arrayOf` fits a list of any length whose items all fit, and `schema/recordOf` a record whose values all fit. Any value that is not a function, a record, or a list fits a value equal to it, so data is a schema for itself:

**Example: Lists and values**

```json
{"a pair": ["schema/fits?",
   ["array/make", 2, "kg"],
   ["array/make", "value/number?", ["schema/anyOf", "kg", "lb"]]],
 "a longer list": ["schema/fits?",
   ["array/make", 2, "kg", "net"],
   ["array/make", "value/number?", "value/string?"]],
 "every item": ["schema/fits?", ["array/make", 1, 2, 3], ["schema/arrayOf", "value/integer?"]],
 "every value": ["schema/problems", {"tea": 2, "cup": "one"}, ["schema/recordOf", "value/integer?"]],
 "the same data": ["schema/fits?", ["quote", {"a": [1, 2]}], ["quote", {"a": [1, 2]}]]}
```

Result:

```json
{
  "a pair": true,
  "a longer list": false,
  "every item": true,
  "every value": [{"path":["cup"],"expected":"value/integer?","found":"one"}],
  "the same data": true
}
```

### Give a schema a name

`schema` declares a schema under a name, the way `relation` declares a relation. The name is then a predicate, and other schemas can use it. A shape can name its own schema, which describes nested data, and one form can declare several schemas that name each other:

**Example: Named schemas**

```json
["begin",
  ["schema", "Line",
    {"sku": "value/string?",
     "qty": ["schema/allOf", "value/integer?",
       ["lambda", ["n"], ["number/greaterThan", "n", 0]]]}],
  ["schema", "Order", {"id": "value/integer?", "lines": ["schema/arrayOf", "Line"]}],
  ["schema", "Folder", {"name": "value/string?", "folders": ["schema/arrayOf", "Folder"]}],
  ["schema",
    "Expr", ["schema/anyOf", "value/number?", "Sum"],
    "Sum", {"add": ["schema/arrayOf", "Expr"]}],
  {"order": ["Order", ["quote", {"id": 1, "lines": [{"sku": "a1", "qty": 2}]}]],
   "expr": ["Expr", ["quote", {"add": [1, {"add": [2, 3]}]}]],
   "bad line": ["schema/problems",
     ["quote", {"id": 1, "lines": [{"sku": "a1", "qty": 0}]}], "Order"],
   "folder": ["Folder",
     ["quote", {"name": "root", "folders": [{"name": "src", "folders": []}]}]]}]
```

Result:

```json
{
  "order": true,
  "expr": true,
  "bad line": [
    {
      "path": ["lines",0,"qty"],
      "expected": ["lambda",["n"],["number/greaterThan","n",0]],
      "found": 0
    }
  ],
  "folder": true
}
```

A lambda is a schema for whatever it returns `true` for. One that fails, as `number/greaterThan` does on a string, simply does not fit. A misspelled name is different: `"value/intger?"` in a shape is an error that suggests `value/integer?`, and not a schema that nothing fits.

### Stop on data that does not fit

`schema/assert` returns the value when it fits, so it can wrap the place where data comes in. When the value does not fit, it fails and says where:

**Example: Assert**

```json
["begin",
  ["schema", "Order", {"id": "value/integer?", "status": ["schema/anyOf", "open", "shipped"]}],
  ["object/get",
    ["schema/assert", ["quote", {"id": 7, "status": "opne"}], "Order"],
    "id"]]
```

Error:

```text
LogicError: {"id":7,"status":"opne"} does not fit "Order": "status" must fit ["schema/anyOf","open","shipped"] but is "opne".
```

### Sort incoming data with rules

A schema check is a call like any other, so it works as a goal in a rule, under `not`, and in a `find`. Here raw documents go in as facts. One rule keeps the ones that fit, and takes them apart with a [pattern](https://lionlang.dev/docs.html#take-data-apart), and another turns each problem of the others into a row:

**Example: In rules**

```json
["begin",
  ["relation", "inbox", ["doc"]],
  ["relation", "order", ["id", "status"], {"key": "id"}],
  ["relation", "rejected", ["doc", "where"]],
  ["schema", "Order", {"id": "value/integer?", "status": ["schema/anyOf", "open", "shipped"]}],
  ["fact",
    ["inbox", {"id": 1, "status": "open"}],
    ["inbox", {"id": 2, "status": "opne"}],
    ["inbox", {"id": "3", "status": "shipped"}]],
  ["rule", ["order", "?id", "?status"],
    ["inbox", ["schema/allOf", "Order", {"id": "?id", "status": "?status"}]]],
  ["rule", ["rejected", "?doc", ["object/get", "?problem", "path"]],
    ["inbox", "?doc"], ["in", "?problem", ["schema/problems", "?doc", "Order"]]],
  {"orders": ["query", ["order", "?id", "?status"]],
   "rejected": ["query", ["rejected", "?doc", "?where"], {"order": "where"}],
   "how many": ["aggregate/count",
     ["find", "?doc", ["and", ["inbox", "?doc"], ["not", ["Order", "?doc"]]]]]}]
```

Result:

```json
{
  "orders": [{"id":1,"status":"open"}],
  "rejected": [
    {"doc":{"id":"3","status":"shipped"},"where":["id"]},
    {"doc":{"id":2,"status":"opne"},"where":["status"]}
  ],
  "how many": 2
}
```

### Have a relation refuse rows that do not fit

The relation option `"schema"` names a declared schema that every row must fit. A row is checked as a record of its columns, so the schema names every column, or is a `schema/open` record that names some. A `fact` form that would add a row that does not fit fails, and changes nothing:

**Example: A relation's schema**

```json
["begin",
  ["schema", "Order", {"id": "value/integer?", "status": ["schema/anyOf", "open", "shipped"]}],
  ["relation", "order", ["id", "status"], {"key": "id", "schema": "Order"}],
  ["fact", ["order", 1, "open"]],
  ["fact", ["order", 2, "opne"]]]
```

Error:

```text
LogicError: Adding this fact breaks an invariant, so nothing changed. The invariant expected no answers but found 1, such as {"id":2,"status":"opne"}: ["and",["order","?id","?status"],["not",["Order",{"id":"?id","status":"?status"}]]]. {"id":2,"status":"opne"} does not fit "Order": "status" must fit ["schema/anyOf","open","shipped"] but is "opne".
```

The option stands for the [invariant](https://lionlang.dev/docs.html#form-invariant) that the message shows, so it is kept like every invariant, and the message ends with where the row does not fit.

### Require that a value exists elsewhere

A relation with one column is a predicate, so it is a schema: a value fits `person` when it is one of its rows. As the schema of a column, that is a foreign key. Retracting a person who is still someone's parent is refused:

**Example: A foreign key**

```json
["begin",
  ["relation", "person", ["name"]],
  ["schema", "Kin", {"parent": "person", "child": "person"}],
  ["relation", "parent", ["parent", "child"], {"schema": "Kin"}],
  ["fact", ["person", "ada"], ["person", "ben"], ["parent", "ada", "ben"]],
  ["retract", ["person", "ben"]]]
```

Error:

```text
LogicError: Retracting this fact breaks an invariant, so nothing changed. The invariant expected no answers but found 1, such as {"parent":"ada","child":"ben"}: ["and",["parent","?parent","?child"],["not",["Kin",{"parent":"?parent","child":"?child"}]]]. {"parent":"ada","child":"ben"} does not fit "Kin": "child" must fit "person" but is "ben".
```

One `fact` form can add a person and their parent together, since a form is checked once it has made all of its changes.

### Check data from TypeScript

Bind the data to a name in the environment, and check it against a schema the database holds:

```ts
import { run } from "@lionlang/core/evaluation/evaluate";
import { LogicDatabase } from "@lionlang/core/logic/database";
import { stdlib } from "@lionlang/core/modules";
import { Effect } from "effect";

const database = new LogicDatabase();
await Effect.runPromise(
  run(["schema", "Order", { id: "value/integer?" }], stdlib, { database })
);

const problems = await Effect.runPromise(
  run(["schema/problems", "incoming", "Order"], { ...stdlib, incoming }, { database })
);
```

An empty list means `incoming` fits. Schemas are data like the rest of a Lion program, so a program can add them while it runs, and a snapshot saves the ones a database holds.

### Related

- [`schema`](https://lionlang.dev/docs.html#form-schema) and [the `schema` module](https://lionlang.dev/docs.html#module-schema) in the reference.
- [Take data apart](https://lionlang.dev/docs.html#take-data-apart) binds logic variables to the parts of a value that fits.
- [Branch on a value's shape](https://lionlang.dev/docs.html#branch-on-shape) uses schemas to choose what to do with a value.
- [Enforce rules on your data](https://lionlang.dev/docs.html#enforce-rules) covers the conditions that span more than one row.
