```json
 "zip": ["array/zip", ["array/make", 1, 2, 3], ["array/make", "a", "b"]],
 "sums of pairs": ["array/map", ["array/zip", ["array/make", 1, 2, 3], ["array/make", 10, 20, 30]], ["lambda", ["pair"], ["aggregate/sum", "pair"]]],
 "includes?": ["array/includes?", ["quote", [1, {"a": 2}]], {"a": 2}],
 "indexOf": ["array/indexOf", ["quote", [1, {"a": 2}, 3]], {"a": 2}],
 "find": ["array/find", ["array/make", 1, 5, 2, 4], ["lambda", ["x"], ["number/greaterThan", "x", 3]]],
 "find fallback": ["array/find", ["array/make", 1, 2], ["lambda", ["x"], ["number/greaterThan", "x", 3]], null],
 "map": ["array/map", ["array/make", 1, 2], ["lambda", ["x"], ["number/add", "x", 1]]],
 "filter": ["array/filter", ["array/make", 1, 5, 2, 4], ["lambda", ["x"], ["number/greaterThan", "x", 2]]],
 "flat-map": ["array/flat-map", ["array/make", 1, 2], ["lambda", ["x"], ["array/make", "x", "x"]]],
 "reverse": ["array/reverse", ["array/make", 1, 2, 3]],
 "sort": ["array/sort", ["array/make", 3, 1, 2]],
 "sort descending": ["array/sort", ["array/make", 3, 1, 2], "number/greaterThan"],
 "reduce": ["array/reduce", ["array/make", 1, 2, 3], 0, ["lambda", ["acc", "x"], ["number/add", "acc", "x"]]],
 "reductions": ["array/reductions", ["array/make", 1, 2, 3], 0, ["lambda", ["acc", "x"], ["number/add", "acc", "x"]]],
 "some?": ["array/some?", ["array/make", 1, 5, 2], ["lambda", ["x"], ["number/greaterThan", "x", 4]]],
 "every?": ["array/every?", ["array/make", 1, 5, 2], ["lambda", ["x"], ["number/greaterThan", "x", 0]]]}
```

Result:

```json
{
  "make": [1,2,3],
  "range": [0,1,2,3],
  "length": 3,
  "head": 1,
  "tail": [2,3],
  "at": 30,
  "at fallback": null,
  "slice": [2,3],
  "lastTwo": [3,4],
  "concat": [1,2,3],
  "zip": [[1,"a"],[2,"b"]],
  "sums of pairs": [11,22,33],
  "includes?": true,
  "indexOf": 1,
  "find": 5,
  "find fallback": null,
  "map": [2,3],
  "filter": [5,4],
  "flat-map": [1,1,2,2],
  "reverse": [3,2,1],
  "sort": [1,2,3],
  "sort descending": [3,2,1],
  "reduce": 6,
  "reductions": [0,1,3,6],
  "some?": true,
  "every?": true
}
```

### value

Predicates tell JSON's kinds of value apart: `value/object?` is true for records, and `value/array?` for lists. `value/unknown?` tells an [unknown](https://lionlang.dev/docs.html#form-some), a value a rule invented, from a value that was given.

| Function | Returns |
| --- | --- |
| `["value/number?", x]` | Whether `x` is a number |
| `["value/integer?", x]` | Whether `x` is a whole number |
| `["value/string?", x]` | Whether `x` is a string |
| `["value/boolean?", x]` | Whether `x` is a boolean. As a schema it lists false and true. |
| `["value/null?", x]` | Whether `x` is `null`. As a schema it lists `null`. |
| `["value/array?", x]` | Whether `x` is a list |
| `["value/object?", x]` | Whether `x` is a record, or another object that is not a list or an unknown, such as a host object |
| `["value/unknown?", x]` | Whether `x` is an [unknown](https://lionlang.dev/docs.html#form-some), such as a value a rule whose head says `exists` invented |
| `["value/function?", x]` | Whether `x` is a function |
| `["value/undefined?", x]` | Whether `x` is JavaScript's `undefined`, which only host values produce |
| `["value/symbol?", x]` | Whether `x` is a JavaScript symbol |
| `["value/any?", x]` | `true` for every value: the schema that anything fits |
| `["value/equals?", a, b]` | Structural equality on any two values, the same rule `=` and `in` use |
| `["value/compare", a, b]` | Total value order (`-1`, `0`, or `1`), the same order `array/sort` and query `"order"` use |
| `["value/identity", x]` | `x` |
| `["value/promise?", x]` | Whether `x` is a promise [`delay`](https://lionlang.dev/docs.html#form-delay) made |
| `["value/force", x]` | The value of a promise: its expression run the first time, and kept, as Racket's `force` gives it; any other `x` as it is |

**Example: value**

```json
{"number?": ["value/number?", 1],
 "integer?": ["value/integer?", 1.5],
 "string?": ["value/string?", "a"],
 "boolean?": ["value/boolean?", false],
 "null?": ["value/null?", null],
 "array?": ["value/array?", ["array/make"]],
 "object? of a record": ["value/object?", {}],
 "object? of a list": ["value/object?", ["array/make"]],
 "function?": ["value/function?", "number/add"],
 "undefined?": ["value/undefined?", null],
 "symbol? of a module's own symbol": ["value/symbol?", "number/symbol"],
 "symbol? of text": ["value/symbol?", ["quote", "number/symbol"]],
 "any?": ["value/any?", null],
 "equals?": ["value/equals?", {"a": 1}, {"a": 1}],
 "compare": ["value/compare", {"a": 1}, {"a": 2}],
 "identity": ["value/identity", 42],
 "promise?": ["value/promise?", ["delay", 1]],
 "force": ["value/force", ["delay", ["number/add", 1, 2]]],
 "force of a plain value": ["value/force", 3]}
```

Result:

```json
{
  "number?": true,
  "integer?": false,
  "string?": true,
  "boolean?": true,
  "null?": true,
  "array?": true,
  "object? of a record": true,
  "object? of a list": false,
  "function?": true,
  "undefined?": false,
  "symbol? of a module's own symbol": true,
  "symbol? of text": false,
  "any?": true,
  "equals?": true,
  "compare": -1,
  "identity": 42,
  "promise?": true,
  "force": 3,
  "force of a plain value": 3
}
```

A rule that invents gives unknowns, and `value/unknown?` keeps them apart from the values that were given:

**Example: value/unknown?**

```json
["begin",
  ["relation", "team", ["name"]],
  ["relation", "lead", ["team", "person"]],
  ["fact", ["team", "web"], ["team", "data"], ["lead", "web", "ana"]],
  ["rule", ["exists", ["?p"], ["lead", "?t", "?p"]], ["team", "?t"]],
  {"leads": ["find", ["array/make", "?t", "?p", ["value/unknown?", "?p"]], ["lead", "?t", "?p"]],
   "known leads": ["find", "?p", ["and", ["lead", "?_", "?p"], ["not", ["value/unknown?", "?p"]]]],
   "object? of an unknown": ["value/object?", ["some", "?p", ["lead", "data", "?p"]]]}]
```

Result:

```json
{
  "leads": [
    ["data",["some","?p",["lead","data","?p"]],true],
    ["web","ana",false]
  ],
  "known leads": ["ana"],
  "object? of an unknown": false
}
```

### schema

Checks values against schemas, and builds schemas out of others. Anything is a schema; see [What fits a schema](https://lionlang.dev/docs.html#schema-fitting). The functions that check take the value first, then the schema. [`schema`](https://lionlang.dev/docs.html#form-schema) gives a schema a name.

| Function | Returns |
| --- | --- |
| `["schema/fits?", value, schema]` | Whether the value fits the schema. With a logic variable in it, it is a goal that also binds the variables of the schema, and binds the value to each value the schema allows when the schema can list them; see [Patterns](https://lionlang.dev/docs.html#logic-patterns). |
| `["schema/problems", value, schema]` | Every place where the value does not fit, in the order of their paths; an empty list when it fits. A problem is a record with a `path`, the keys and positions that lead to the part. A part with the wrong value has what was `expected`, a schema written as the expression that makes it, and what was `found`. A part that is missing has only `expected`, and a key the schema does not name has only `found`. |
| `["schema/includes?", a, b]` | Whether every value `a` allows fits `b`: decided exactly, by listing `a`'s values when it can list them and by the [solver](https://lionlang.dev/docs.html#logic-solving) otherwise. Fails, and says why, when neither can decide it. |
| `["schema/assert", value, schema]` | The value, when it fits. When it does not, fails with a message that says where. As a value in a rule or `find`, it fails the query that runs it. |
| `["schema/anyOf", schema, ...]` | A schema that fits a value which fits at least one of the schemas. Of plain values it is a list of choices. It reports one problem, at the value that fits none. |
| `["schema/allOf", schema, ...]` | A schema that fits a value which fits every one of the schemas. It reports the problems of each schema the value does not fit. |
| `["schema/arrayOf", schema]` `["schema/arrayOf", schema, most]` | A schema that fits a list whose every item fits the schema. With `most`, a whole number, the list has at most that many items, so a schema whose items can be listed lists every such list. |
| `["schema/recordOf", schema]` | A schema that fits a record whose every value fits the schema |
| `["schema/optional", schema]` | As the schema of a record's key, lets the key be left out; a key that is there must fit. Anywhere else it is the schema itself. |
| `["schema/open", record]` `["schema/open", record, rest]` | A schema that fits a record which fits the record of schemas, or the named schema of one, whatever other keys it has. With `rest`, the record of its other keys must fit `rest`. A list of schemas works the same way, with the items after the ones it names as the rest. A record or list of schemas on its own leaves nothing for its rest. |

What the building functions return is a function: called with a value, it says whether the value fits. A snapshot writes it as the call that built it.

**Example: schema**

```json
{"fits?": ["schema/fits?", 3, "value/number?"],
 "problems": ["schema/problems",
   {"id": "x"},
   {"id": "value/integer?", "name": "value/string?"}],
 "assert": ["schema/assert", 3, "value/number?"],
 "includes?": ["schema/includes?", "value/integer?", "value/number?"],
 "numbers not all whole": ["schema/includes?", "value/number?", "value/integer?"],
 "strings not numbers": ["schema/includes?", "value/string?", "value/number?"],
 "anyOf": ["schema/fits?", null, ["schema/anyOf", "value/string?", null]],
 "allOf": ["schema/fits?", 5,
   ["schema/allOf", "value/integer?", ["lambda", ["n"], ["number/lessThan", "n", 3]]]],
 "arrayOf": ["schema/fits?", ["array/make", 1, 2], ["schema/arrayOf", "value/number?"]],
 "at most two": ["schema/fits?", ["array/make", 1, 2, 3], ["schema/arrayOf", "value/number?", 2]],
 "every value": ["find", "?x", ["schema/fits?", "?x", {"on": "value/boolean?", "size": ["schema/anyOf", "s", "m"]}]],
 "recordOf": ["schema/fits?", {"a": 1, "b": "x"}, ["schema/recordOf", "value/number?"]],
 "optional": ["schema/fits?", {}, {"note": ["schema/optional", "value/string?"]}],
 "extra key": ["schema/problems", {"id": 1, "extra": true}, {"id": "value/integer?"}],
 "open": ["schema/fits?", {"id": 1, "extra": true}, ["schema/open", {"id": "value/integer?"}]],
 "open with a rest": ["schema/problems", {"id": 1, "size": "m", "count": 2},
   ["schema/open", {"id": "value/integer?"}, ["schema/recordOf", "value/string?"]]],
 "called": [["schema/arrayOf", "value/number?"], ["array/make", 1, "two"]]}
```

Result:

```json
{
  "fits?": true,
  "problems": [
    {"path":["id"],"expected":"value/integer?","found":"x"},
    {"path":["name"],"expected":"value/string?"}
  ],
  "assert": 3,
  "includes?": true,
  "numbers not all whole": false,
  "strings not numbers": false,
  "anyOf": true,
  "allOf": false,
  "arrayOf": true,
  "at most two": false,
  "every value": [
    {"on":false,"size":"m"},
    {"on":false,"size":"s"},
    {"on":true,"size":"m"},
    {"on":true,"size":"s"}
  ],
  "recordOf": false,
  "optional": true,
  "extra key": [{"path":["extra"],"found":true}],
  "open": true,
  "open with a rest": [{"path":["count"],"expected":"value/string?","found":2}],
  "called": false
}
```

**Example: A value that does not fit**

```json
["schema/assert",
  {"id": 7, "tags": ["array/make", "new", 3]},
  {"id": "value/integer?", "tags": ["schema/arrayOf", "value/string?"]}]
```

Error:

```text
LogicError: {"id":7,"tags":["new",3]} does not fit {"id":"value/integer?","tags":["schema/arrayOf","value/string?"]}: "tags.1" must fit "value/string?" but is 3.
```

### object

For records and host objects. Paths are dot-separated keys; a numeric segment indexes a list. Keys belong to objects, so reading one needs an object, but a method can belong to any value except `null`, so the method functions also work on strings, numbers, and lists.

| Function | Returns |
| --- | --- |
| `["object/get", object, key, missing?]` | The value under a `key` the object has, `null` among them. For a key it does not have, `missing`, as Racket's `hash-ref` takes a failure result; without it the call fails with `KeyNotFoundError`, as `object/get-path` does. Only the object's own keys count. Fails with `NotAnObjectError` for a non-object. |
| `["object/has?", record, key]` | Whether the record has the key, as Racket's `hash-has-key?` says: `true` for a key that holds `null`, and `false` for one it does not have. |
| `["object/get-path", object, path]` | The value at `path`, such as `"users.1.name"`. Fails with `KeyNotFoundError`, `IndexOutOfBoundsError`, `NotAnArrayError`, or `PathTraversalError` when the path does not lead to a value. |
| `["object/keys", record]` | The record's keys |
| `["object/values", record]` | The record's values |
| `["object/entries", record]` | The record's `[key, value]` pairs |
| `["object/fromEntries", pairs]` | A record built from `[key, value]` pairs; refuses `"__proto__"` |
| `["object/set", record, key, value]` | A new record with `key` holding `value`, as `hash-set` gives in Racket. The record it was given is unchanged. |
| `["object/remove", record, key]` | A new record without `key`, as `hash-remove` gives in Racket. Removing a key the record does not hold gives the same record. |
| `["object/merge", record, ...]` | A new record combining zero or more records left to right (later keys override earlier ones) |
| `["object/json-stringify", value, replacer, space]` | Any JSON value as JSON text, like `JSON.stringify`. The replacer and the indent are optional. |
| `["object/json-parse", text]` | Parses JSON text into a Lion value, keeping decimals and large integers exact |
| `["object/call-method", value, name, argument, ...]` | The result of calling `value`'s method `name`. Fails with `NotAFunctionError` when there is no such method, and `NotAnObjectError` when `value` is `null`. |
| `["object/get-method", value, name]` | The method `name` of `value`, bound to it. Fails like `object/call-method`. |
| `["object/call-method-path", object, path, argument, ...]` | The result of calling the method at the end of `path`, with `this` set to the value before it. Every value the path passes through must be an object; the last can be any value except `null`. |
| `["object/get-method-path", object, path]` | The method at the end of `path`, bound to the value before it |
| `["object/new", class, argument, ...]` | A new instance of `class`. Fails with `NotAConstructorError` for a non-function. |

**Example: object**

```json
["begin",
  ["define", "data", ["quote", {"users": [{"name": "ana"}, {"name": "bo"}], "port": 8080}]],
  {"get": ["object/get", "data", "port"],
   "get-path": ["object/get-path", "data", "users.1.name"],
   "keys": ["object/keys", "data"],
   "values": ["object/values", ["quote", {"a": 1, "b": 2}]],
   "entries": ["object/entries", ["quote", {"a": 1, "b": 2}]],
   "fromEntries": ["object/fromEntries", ["quote", [["a", 1], ["b", 2]]]],
   "set": ["object/set", ["quote", {"a": 1}], "b", 2],
   "remove": ["object/remove", ["quote", {"a": 1, "b": 2}], "a"],
   "merge": ["object/merge", ["quote", {"a": 1, "b": 2}], ["quote", {"b": 3, "c": 4}]],
   "keys without port": ["object/keys", ["object/remove", "data", "port"]],
   "json-stringify": ["object/json-stringify", ["quote", {"a": [1, 2]}], null, 0],
   "json-parse exact": ["number/add", ["object/get", ["object/json-parse", "{\"x\": 0.1}"], "x"], 0.2],
   "missing, with a value to use": ["object/get", "data", "host", "localhost"],
   "has?": ["object/has?", "data", "port"],
   "has? a key that holds null": ["object/has?", ["quote", {"host": null}], "host"],
   "call-method": ["object/call-method", "lion", "toUpperCase"],
   "call-method-path": ["object/call-method-path", "data", "users.0.name.toUpperCase"],
   "get-method": [["object/get-method", ["array/make", 1, 2], "join"], "+"],
   "get-method-path": [["object/get-method-path", "data", "users.1.name.padStart"], 4, "."]}]
```

Result:

```json
{
  "get": 8080,
  "get-path": "bo",
  "keys": ["users","port"],
  "values": [1,2],
  "entries": [["a",1],["b",2]],
  "fromEntries": {"a":1,"b":2},
  "set": {"a":1,"b":2},
  "remove": {"b":2},
  "merge": {"a":1,"b":3,"c":4},
  "keys without port": ["users"],
  "json-stringify": "{\"a\":[1,2]}",
  "json-parse exact": 0.3,
  "missing, with a value to use": "localhost",
  "has?": true,
  "has? a key that holds null": true,
  "call-method": "LION",
  "call-method-path": "ANA",
  "get-method": "1+2",
  "get-method-path": "..bo"
}
```

`object/new` constructs a class that host code binds, as in [Call host objects](https://lionlang.dev/docs.html#call-host-objects). A value that is not a class fails:

**Example: object/new without a class**

```json
["object/new", 42]
```

Error:

```text
NotAConstructorError: Expected a class to construct, but found 42.
```

### quantity

Numbers that carry their units, checked when the program runs, as Pint checks them. A quantity is data: a record of a `value` and a `unit`, the unit a record from each base unit's name to its whole exponent, so `{"value": 15, "unit": {"m": 1, "s": -1}}` is 15 metres a second. A plain number is a quantity with no unit, and a result with no unit left is its plain number. Units are equal when their records are; to convert, multiply by a quantity such as `{"value": 1000, "unit": {"m": 1, "km": -1}}`. A quantity is a record, so a schema says what unit a value has: `{"value": "value/number?", "unit": {"m": 1}}`.

| Function | Returns |
| --- | --- |
| `["quantity/add", a, b, ...]` | The sum of quantities of one unit, in that unit; quantities of different units fail with `ArithmeticError` |
| `["quantity/subtract", a, b]` | The difference of two quantities of one unit |
| `["quantity/multiply", a, b, ...]` | The product: the values multiplied, each base unit's exponents added |
| `["quantity/divide", a, b]` | The quotient: the values divided, the divisor's exponents taken away |
| `["quantity/power", a, n]` | `a` to the whole power `n`: each exponent multiplied by `n` |
| `["quantity/in", a, unit]` | The number `a` is in `unit`, when that is its unit; any other unit fails |

**Example: quantity**

```json
["begin",
  ["define", "distance", ["quote", {"value": 120, "unit": {"m": 1}}]],
  ["define", "duration", ["quote", {"value": 8, "unit": {"s": 1}}]],
  ["define", "metres per km", ["quote", {"value": 1000, "unit": {"m": 1, "km": -1}}]],
  {"speed": ["quantity/divide", "distance", "duration"],
   "twice as far": ["quantity/add", "distance", "distance"],
   "a little less": ["quantity/subtract", "distance", ["quote", {"value": 20, "unit": {"m": 1}}]],
   "back to a distance": ["quantity/multiply", ["quantity/divide", "distance", "duration"], "duration"],
   "no unit left": ["quantity/divide", "distance", "distance"],
   "area": ["quantity/power", "distance", 2],
   "in km": ["quantity/in", ["quantity/divide", "distance", "metres per km"], {"km": 1}],
   "farther than 100 m?": ["number/greaterThan", ["quantity/in", "distance", {"m": 1}], 100]}]
```

Result:

```json
{
  "speed": {"value":15,"unit":{"m":1,"s":-1}},
  "twice as far": {"value":240,"unit":{"m":1}},
  "a little less": {"value":100,"unit":{"m":1}},
  "back to a distance": {"value":120,"unit":{"m":1}},
  "no unit left": 1,
  "area": {"value":14400,"unit":{"m":2}},
  "in km": 0.12,
  "farther than 100 m?": true
}
```

A length and a time cannot be added:

**Example: quantity/add of different units**

```json
["quantity/add", ["quote", {"value": 120, "unit": {"m": 1}}], ["quote", {"value": 8, "unit": {"s": 1}}]]
```

Error:

```text
ArithmeticError: quantity/add: 120 {"m":1} and 8 {"s":1} have different units.
```

### func

For working with functions, especially host functions.

| Function | Returns |
| --- | --- |
| `["func/partial", function, argument, ...]` | A function that calls `function` with these arguments followed by its own, exactly as a call written out in full would. Made from a relation, it builds goals, as the relation does. Made from a logic variable in a rule or query, it waits for the variable, so `["func/partial", "number/lessThan", "?max"]` is a [predicate](https://lionlang.dev/docs.html#logic-patterns) for values above `?max`. |
| `["func/catch", thunk, handler]` | What `thunk`, a function of no arguments, gives; when it fails, what `handler` gives for the failure as data, as Racket's `with-handlers`: `{"failure": kind, "message": text}`, and for a failure `func/raise` made, `"failure": "raised"` and the `value`. A call that waits for a logic variable is no failure |
| `["func/raise", value]` | Fails with `value`, as Racket's `raise`: its message is the value, a string as it is, and `func/catch` gives back the value |
| `["func/reset", thunk]` | What `thunk`, a function of no arguments, gives, or what the handler of a `func/shift` inside it gives: the delimited part of a continuation, as Racket's `reset` |
| `["func/shift", handler]` | Stops the delimited part where it stands; its `func/reset` gives what `handler` gives for `k`, the rest of the delimited part. A call of `k` with a value resumes it there, once, and gives what the rest gives, as Racket's `shift`, but resumed once |
| `["func/apply", function, this, argument, ..., list]` | What calling `function` with `this`, the arguments, and then the items of `list` returns, as Scheme's `apply` spreads its last argument |
| `["func/bind", function, this, argument, ...]` | `function` with `this` and leading arguments fixed |
| `["func/callback", function]` | A JavaScript function that calls `function` with as many of the arguments it is given as `function` takes, and returns its result, or a Promise of it when the work is asynchronous. The callback keeps the environment and database it was created in. |

**Example: func**

```json
{"partial": [["func/partial", "number/add", 10], 5],
 "apply": ["func/apply", "number/subtract", null, ["array/make", 10, 4]],
 "apply after one": ["func/apply", "number/add", null, 1, ["array/make", 2, 3]],
 "bind": [["func/bind", "number/multiply", null, 3], 7],
 "callback": ["value/function?", ["func/callback", "number/add"]]}
```

Result:

```json
{
  "partial": 15,
  "apply": 6,
  "apply after one": 6,
  "bind": 21,
  "callback": true
}
```

A continuation stops a computation and resumes it later: an early exit, a resumed one, and a generator that yields its items one at a time:

**Example: func/reset and func/shift**

```json
["begin",
  ["define", "generator", ["lambda", ["items"],
    ["func/reset", ["lambda", [],
      ["begin",
        ["array/map", "items", ["lambda", ["item"], ["func/shift", ["lambda", ["k"], {"value": "item", "rest": "k"}]]]],
        {"value": null, "rest": null}]]]]],
  ["define", "first", ["generator", ["array/make", "a", "b"]]],
  ["define", "second", [["object/get", "first", "rest"], null]],
  {"early exit": ["func/reset", ["lambda", [], ["number/add", 1, ["func/shift", ["lambda", ["k"], 42]]]]],
   "resumed": ["func/reset", ["lambda", [], ["number/add", 1, ["func/shift", ["lambda", ["k"], ["number/multiply", 10, ["k", 5]]]]]]],
   "yielded": ["array/make", ["object/get", "first", "value"], ["object/get", "second", "value"]]}]
```

Result:

```json
{"early exit":42,"resumed":60,"yielded":["a","b"]}
```

A failure is data a program can catch, read, and raise:

**Example: func/catch**

```json
["begin",
  ["define", "safe divide", ["lambda", ["a", "b"],
    ["func/catch", ["lambda", [], ["number/divide", "a", "b"]],
      ["lambda", ["failure"], {"failed": ["object/get", "failure", "message"]}]]]],
  ["define", "checked", ["lambda", ["n"],
    ["cond", [["number/lessThan", "n", 0], ["func/raise", {"code": "negative", "n": "n"}]], ["else", "n"]]]],
  {"divided": ["safe divide", 6, 3],
   "by zero": ["safe divide", 1, 0],
   "raised": ["func/catch", ["lambda", [], ["checked", -2]], ["lambda", ["failure"], "failure"]]}]
```

Result:

```json
{
  "divided": 2,
  "by zero": {"failed":"number/divide: 1 ÷ 0 has no finite result."},
  "raised": {
    "failure": "raised",
    "message": "{\"code\":\"negative\",\"n\":-2}",
    "value": {"code":"negative","n":-2}
  }
}
```

### console

Effects for output. On this page, output appears above the result.

| Function | Returns |
| --- | --- |
| `["console/log", message]` | Prints `message` and returns it |
| `["console/log-json", value]` | Prints `value` as indented JSON and returns that text |

**Example: console**

```json
["begin",
  ["console/log", "starting"],
  ["console/log-json", {"step": 1}],
  "done"]
```

Result:

```json
"done"
```

### aggregate

Called on a list, each function combines the list. Called on anything else, it waits for the list its argument turns out to be; a [`find`](https://lionlang.dev/docs.html#form-find) is the list of what it found. Only as a whole argument of a rule's head, and not on a `find`, it combines one value from each of the rule's matches instead, grouped by the head's other columns; see [Summarize groups of facts](https://lionlang.dev/docs.html#summarize-groups). Each function takes exactly one argument.

| Function | Returns | Of nothing |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `["aggregate/count", values]` | How many values | `0` |
| `["aggregate/countUnique", values]` | How many distinct values | `0` |
| `["aggregate/sum", values]` | The exact sum, so the order of the values never changes it; values must be numbers | `0` |
| `["aggregate/mean", values]` | The exact mean: the sum divided by how many values there are, which may be a fraction such as 7/3; values must be numbers | `null` |
| `["aggregate/median", values]` | The exact median: the middle number for an odd count, or the exact midpoint of the two middle numbers for an even count; values must be numbers | `null` |
| `["aggregate/argMin", pairs]` | The value of the `[key, value]` pair with the smallest key (all numbers or all strings); ties go to the smaller value | `null` |
| `["aggregate/argMax", pairs]` | The value of the `[key, value]` pair with the largest key (all numbers or all strings); ties go to the smaller value | `null` |
| `["aggregate/min", values]` | The smallest; all numbers or all strings. Lattice. | `null` |
| `["aggregate/max", values]` | The largest; all numbers or all strings. Lattice. | `null` |
| `["aggregate/shortest", values]` | The shortest list or string; ties go to the smaller value. Lattice. | `null` |
| `["aggregate/union", values]` | Every item of every list, distinct and sorted. Lattice. | `[]` |
| `["aggregate/collect", values]` | Every value, sorted, duplicates kept | `[]` |
| `["aggregate/unique", values]` | The distinct values, sorted | `[]` |

A sum is exact, so adding the same numbers in another order, as the matches of a rule or the candidates of a key may come, gives the same number:

**Example: A sum in any order**

```json
{"forward": ["aggregate/sum", ["array/make", 1e16, 0.1, -1e16, 0.2]],
 "backward": ["aggregate/sum", ["array/make", 0.2, -1e16, 0.1, 1e16]]}
```

Result:

```json
{"forward":0.3,"backward":0.3}
```

Lattice aggregates only move one way as values arrive, so they may aggregate through recursion. See [Logic database guarantees](https://lionlang.dev/docs.html#logic-guarantees).

**Example: aggregate**

```json
["begin",
  ["define", "values", ["array/make", 3, 1, 3, 2]],
  {"count": ["aggregate/count", "values"],
   "countUnique": ["aggregate/countUnique", "values"],
   "sum": ["aggregate/sum", "values"],
   "mean": ["aggregate/mean", "values"],
   "median": ["aggregate/median", "values"],
   "argMin": ["aggregate/argMin", ["quote", [[2024, "draft"], [2025, "final"]]]],
   "argMax": ["aggregate/argMax", ["quote", [[2024, "draft"], [2025, "final"]]]],
   "min": ["aggregate/min", "values"],
   "max": ["aggregate/max", "values"],
   "shortest": ["aggregate/shortest", ["quote", [[1, 2], [3], "ab"]]],
   "union": ["aggregate/union", ["quote", [[2, 1], [3, 1]]]],
   "collect": ["aggregate/collect", "values"],
   "unique": ["aggregate/unique", "values"]}]
```

Result:

```json
{
  "count": 4,
  "countUnique": 3,
  "sum": 9,
  "mean": 2.25,
  "median": 2.5,
  "argMin": "draft",
  "argMax": "final",
  "min": 1,
  "max": 3,
  "shortest": [3],
  "union": [1,2,3],
  "collect": [1,2,3,3],
  "unique": [1,2,3]
}
```

### graph

Algorithms over an edge relation whose first two columns are from and to. Each call is a goal: give the edge relation, any other inputs, then one term per output column. An input is a value, or a variable that another goal binds; the algorithm then runs once for each value. Results never depend on the order facts were added.

| Goal | Rows |
| --- | --- |
| `["graph/shortestPath", edges, start, to, cost, path]` | Dijkstra's algorithm from `start`, in order of cost, starting with `start` itself at cost 0. A third edge column is the weight, at least 0; without one, each edge costs 1. |
| `["graph/simplePaths", edges, start, end, maxHops, cost, path]` | Every cycle-free directed path from `start` to `end` of at most `maxHops` edges, with optional non-negative third-column weights, ordered by cost then path |
| `["graph/lca", edges, a, b, lca, distA, distB]` | Lowest (most specific) common ancestors of `a` and `b` in a DAG following edges from child to parent, with shortest hop distances from `a` and `b` |
| `["graph/dominators", edges, start, node, dominator]` | Immediate dominator tree for every node reachable from `start` (excluding `start` itself, so the output edges form a rooted tree DAG) |
| `["graph/influence", edges, start, to, weight]` | Exact weighted influence from `start` to each reachable node: sum over all directed simple paths of the product of edge weights (optional third column, defaulting to 1) |
| `["graph/pageRank", edges, node, rank]` | PageRank with damping 0.85, rounded to 6 decimal places. Ranks add up to 1. |
| `["graph/betweenness", edges, node, score]` | Directed betweenness centrality by Brandes's algorithm, rounded to 6 decimal places. A third edge column is a non-negative weight; without one, each edge costs 1. |
| `["graph/components", edges, node, component]` | Connected components, ignoring direction, named after their smallest node |
| `["graph/stronglyConnected", edges, node, component]` | Strongly connected components, named after their smallest node |
| `["graph/cycles", edges, component, cycle]` | One canonical shortest directed cycle per cyclic strongly connected component (including self-loops), named after its smallest node; empty on an acyclic graph |
| `["graph/transitiveReduction", edges, from, to]` | The unique minimal edge set of a DAG with the same reachability (Hasse diagram), or an error naming a cycle |
| `["graph/topologicalOrder", edges, node, position]` | Positions from 0 in a topological order, or an error that names a cycle |

**Example: graph**

```json
["begin",
  ["relation", "edge", ["from", "to"]],
  ["fact", ["edge", "a", "b"], ["edge", "b", "c"], ["edge", "c", "d"], ["edge", "a", "c"]],
  {"shortestPath": ["query", ["graph/shortestPath", "edge", "a", "d", "?cost", "?path"]],
   "simplePaths": ["query", ["graph/simplePaths", "edge", "a", "d", 3, "?cost", "?path"], {"order": ["cost", "path"]}],
   "lca": ["query", ["graph/lca", "edge", "a", "b", "?lca", "?da", "?db"]],
   "dominators": ["query", ["graph/dominators", "edge", "a", "?node", "?dom"], {"order": "node"}],
   "influence": ["query", ["graph/influence", "edge", "a", "?node", "?weight"], {"order": "node"}],
   "pageRank": ["query", ["graph/pageRank", "edge", "?node", "?rank"], {"order": "-rank", "limit": 1}],
   "betweenness": ["query", ["graph/betweenness", "edge", "?node", "?score"], {"order": "-score", "limit": 1}],
   "components": ["query", ["graph/components", "edge", "?node", "?c"], {"limit": 1}],
   "stronglyConnected": ["query", ["graph/stronglyConnected", "edge", "c", "?c"]],
   "cycles": ["query", ["graph/cycles", "edge", "?component", "?cycle"]],
   "transitiveReduction": ["query", ["graph/transitiveReduction", "edge", "?from", "?to"], {"order": ["from", "to"]}],
   "topologicalOrder": ["query", ["graph/topologicalOrder", "edge", "?node", "?position"], {"order": "position"}]}]
```

Result:

```json
{
  "shortestPath": [{"cost":2,"path":["a","c","d"]}],
  "simplePaths": [
    {"cost":2,"path":["a","c","d"]},
    {"cost":3,"path":["a","b","c","d"]}
  ],
  "lca": [{"lca":"b","da":1,"db":0}],
  "dominators": [
    {"node":"b","dom":"a"},
    {"node":"c","dom":"a"},
    {"node":"d","dom":"c"}
  ],
  "influence": [
    {"node":"b","weight":1},
    {"node":"c","weight":2},
    {"node":"d","weight":2}
  ],
  "pageRank": [{"node":"d","rank":0.390362}],
  "betweenness": [{"node":"c","score":2}],
  "components": [{"node":"a","c":"a"}],
  "stronglyConnected": [{"c":"c"}],
  "cycles": [],
  "transitiveReduction": [
    {"from":"a","to":"b"},
    {"from":"b","to":"c"},
    {"from":"c","to":"d"}
  ],
  "topologicalOrder": [
    {"node":"a","position":0},
    {"node":"b","position":1},
    {"node":"c","position":2},
    {"node":"d","position":3}
  ]
}
```

### `proof`

Checks proof values with a small trusted kernel (without invoking the solver), proves universal or empirical goals, computes exact tight symbolic and relational bounds, and proves universal properties of rule-defined relations by rule induction. See [Prove that every command keeps a rule](https://lionlang.dev/docs.html#prove-commands).

#### `proof/valid?`

Whether a proof value (linear refutation certificate, Omega integer split tree, case split, induction proof, lemma composition, proof/prove or proof/bounds result, or why derivation) checks out under the trusted kernel. With a second claim argument (such as {"atLeast": 0.28}, a relation name, or a ground fact), also checks that the proof establishes that exact claim.

#### `proof/prove`

Proves a universal (["not", ["exists", ...]]) or empirical goal, returning a kernel-verifiable proof (with facts and assumptions for database derivations) or a concrete counterexample witness when a universal claim fails.

#### `proof/bounds`

Computes exact tight min and max bounds of an expression subject to a goal across continuous linear, mixed-integer linear, integer & continuous linear-fractional ratios (Charnes-Cooper & Dinkelbach), bilinear/quadratic products, and relational database constraints, returning endpoint witnesses and kernel-checkable minProof / maxProof certificates.

#### `proof/sensitivity`

All-derivations epistemic fragility analysis for a closed goal: identifies single-point-of-failure critical facts, redundant facts backed by alternative derivations, resilient status, and minimal size-1/size-2 retraction cut-sets (minimalCuts).

#### `proof/rules`

Takes a relation and a target schema, or a record mapping mutually recursive relation names to schemas, and proves by rule induction that every derived row fits its schema across all databases whose base relations fit their declared schemas (including single-column schema invariants, nested pattern destructuring, and aggregate output domains).

#### `proof/facts`

Returns the sorted, deduplicated list of recorded (given: true) base facts that a why explanation rests on.

#### `proof/assumptions`

Returns the sorted, deduplicated list of leaf absent goals (closed-world negative premises or missing facts) that a why explanation rests on.

**Example: proof**

```json
["begin",
  ["schema", "PosRow", {"id": "value/string?", "score": ["schema/allOf", "value/integer?", ["lambda", ["n"], ["number/greaterThanOrEqualTo", "n", 1]]]}],
  ["relation", "base", ["id", "score"], {"schema": "PosRow"}],
  ["relation", "blocked", ["id"]],
  ["relation", "reach", ["id", "score"]],
  ["fact", ["base", "a", 2]],
  ["rule", ["reach", "?x", ["aggregate/min", "?s"]], ["base", "?x", "?s"], ["not", ["blocked", "?x"]]],
  ["rule", ["reach", "?x", ["aggregate/min", ["number/add", "?s", 1]]], ["reach", "?x", "?s"]],
  ["define", "p", ["proof/rules", "reach", "PosRow"]],
  ["define", "w", ["why", ["reach", "a", 2]]],
  ["define", "b", ["proof/bounds",
    ["number/divide", ["number/subtract", "?r", "?c"], "?r"],
    ["and",
      ["schema/fits?", "?r", "value/number?"], ["schema/fits?", "?c", "value/number?"],
      ["number/greaterThanOrEqualTo", "?r", 238], ["number/lessThanOrEqualTo", "?r", 242],
      ["number/greaterThanOrEqualTo", "?c", 161], ["number/lessThanOrEqualTo", "?c", 165]]]],
  ["define", "cov", ["proof/prove", ["not", ["exists", ["?r", "?c"],
    ["and",
      ["schema/fits?", "?r", "value/number?"], ["schema/fits?", "?c", "value/number?"],
      ["number/greaterThanOrEqualTo", "?r", 238], ["number/lessThanOrEqualTo", "?r", 242],
      ["number/greaterThanOrEqualTo", "?c", 161], ["number/lessThanOrEqualTo", "?c", 165],
      ["number/lessThan", ["number/divide", ["number/subtract", "?r", "?c"], "?r"], 0.32]]]]]],
  {"rulesProved": ["object/get", "p", "proved"],
   "rulesValid": ["proof/valid?", "p"],
   "minPct": ["number/round", ["number/multiply", 100, ["object/get", "b", "min"]], 2],
   "maxPct": ["number/round", ["number/multiply", 100, ["object/get", "b", "max"]], 2],
   "boundsValid": ["proof/valid?", "b"],
   "boundsClear30": ["proof/valid?", "b", {"atLeast": 0.30}],
   "sensitivity": ["proof/sensitivity", ["reach", "a", 2]],
   "covenantProved": ["object/get", "cov", "proved"],
   "counterexample": ["object/get", "cov", "counterexample"],
   "facts": ["proof/facts", "w"],
   "assumptions": ["proof/assumptions", "w"]}]
```

Result:

```json
{
  "rulesProved": true,
  "rulesValid": true,
  "minPct": 30.67,
  "maxPct": 33.47,
  "boundsValid": true,
  "boundsClear30": true,
  "sensitivity": {
    "critical": [["base","a",2]],
    "holds": true,
    "minCutSize": 1,
    "minimalCuts": [[["base","a",2]]],
    "redundant": [],
    "resilient": false
  },
  "covenantProved": false,
  "counterexample": {"?r":238,"?c":162},
  "facts": [["base","a",2]],
  "assumptions": [["blocked","a"]]
}
```

### `time`

Deterministic proleptic Gregorian UTC calendar and timestamp functions, with zero dependence on the host's local time zone. Instants are exact integer UTC milliseconds since `1970-01-01T00:00:00.000Z`.

| Call | Gives |
| --- | --- |
| `["time/parse", text]` | Exact integer UTC epoch milliseconds for an ISO-8601 date (`"2026-03-03"`) or timestamp with explicit zone (`"2026-03-03T11:40:00-05:00"`, `"2026-03-03 16:40 UTC"`), or `null` when invalid |
| `["time/fromParts", year, month, day, hour?, minute?, second?, offsetMinutes?]` | Exact integer UTC epoch milliseconds from Gregorian calendar parts, failing on impossible dates |
| `["time/format", epochMs]` `["time/format", epochMs, precision]` | ISO-8601 UTC string at `"date"`, `"minute"`, `"second"` (default), or `"ms"` |
| `["time/parts", epochMs]` | Record `{"year", "month", "day", "hour", "minute", "second", "ms", "dayOfWeek"}` in UTC (`dayOfWeek` 0=Sunday..6=Saturday) |
| `["time/diff", endMs, startMs]` `["time/diff", endMs, startMs, unit]` | Exact elapsed duration `endMs - startMs` in `"ms"` (default), `"seconds"`, `"minutes"`, `"hours"`, or `"days"` |
| `["time/add", epochMs, amount, unit]` | Shifts `epochMs` by an exact `amount` in `"ms"`, `"seconds"`, `"minutes"`, `"hours"`, or `"days"` |

**Example: time**

```json
["begin",
  ["define", "detected", ["time/parse", "2026-03-03T14:05:00Z"]],
  ["define", "mitigated", ["time/parse", "2026-03-03T11:40:00-05:00"]],
  {"sameAsFromParts": ["=", "mitigated", ["time/fromParts", 2026, 3, 3, 11, 40, 0, -300]],
   "elapsedMinutes": ["time/diff", "mitigated", "detected", "minutes"],
   "nextDay": ["time/format", ["time/add", "mitigated", 1, "days"], "minute"],
   "parts": ["time/parts", "mitigated"]}]
```

Result:

```json
{
  "sameAsFromParts": true,
  "elapsedMinutes": 155,
  "nextDay": "2026-03-04T16:40Z",
  "parts": {
    "year": 2026,
    "month": 3,
    "day": 3,
    "hour": 16,
    "minute": 40,
    "second": 0,
    "ms": 0,
    "dayOfWeek": 2
  }
}
```

### Module symbols

Every module except `console` also binds `module/symbol`, such as `number/symbol`, to a JavaScript symbol that identifies the module.

---

## Logic database guarantees

URL: https://lionlang.dev/docs.html#logic-guarantees
Section: Reference (Reference)

> The rules every logic program follows, what Lion checks and when, and what it promises about changes and answers.

The logic database checks rules, goals, and changes as they arrive, so that every program has one well-defined answer, evaluation always finishes, and the data never ends up half changed.

### Safety

- Every variable in a rule's head must be bound by a goal in its body, unless the head lists it in [`exists`](https://lionlang.dev/docs.html#form-exists). A variable that `exists` lists cannot also be bound by the body.
- Every variable in a filter or in a computed value must first be bound by a relation goal, `=`, `in`, or `schema/fits?`, or typed by a schema that says what kind its values are, such as `value/integer?`, so that it is [solved for](https://lionlang.dev/docs.html#logic-solving). Every variable in an input of a graph algorithm must be bound, and an input must be data. An array is always a call, so a list pattern written as `["?a", "?b"]` calls `?a` and binds nothing: write it `["array/make", "?a", "?b"]`, as the message of a goal that cannot run says.
- `schema/fits?` binds the value it checks only when nothing else can. A schema that [lists the values it allows](https://lionlang.dev/docs.html#logic-patterns) binds it to each, at most 100,000 of them. One that says what kind they are, such as `value/integer?`, makes the variable symbolic: the filters about it are [solved for](https://lionlang.dev/docs.html#logic-solving), and the ones the solver cannot decide wait for the values it lists. A variable no goal binds and no such schema types stays unbound, and the message says why.
- A [question](https://lionlang.dev/docs.html#logic-asking), a goal under `not`, a goal used as a value, or a `find`, waits for the variables that the rule or query around it binds. Every other variable in it is its own, and the question must bind it itself. A `find` must bind every variable of its template.
- The list in `in` must be bound before it runs.
- Lion orders the goals of a body so each runs once its inputs are bound. Filters that are ready together run in the order written, so a guard written first protects the filter after it. Otherwise the order you write goals in only matters for [goal-directed queries](https://lionlang.dev/docs.html#goal-directed-evaluation).

A rule, query, or invariant that breaks a safety rule fails when it is added or run, with a message that names the unbound variable.

### Values

- A value computed from a logic variable is what the same expression gives with the variable's value in its place. This holds for every function, for `cond`, `match`, `eval`, and records, for lambdas, and for the questions an expression asks: a goal used as a value and a `find` give in a rule what they give in plain code.
- A filter must be `true` or `false`. The rows a rule derives and the answers a query gives must be data: JSON values and [unknowns](https://lionlang.dev/docs.html#form-some). Anything else fails with an error that shows the call or the value.
- A function that fails while a rule or query runs it fails the rule or query. A function given a value it does not take names itself, the argument, and the value, as in plain code; any other failure names the call and the values it ran on.
- Whether a value [fits](https://lionlang.dev/docs.html#schema-fitting) a schema is the same wherever it is asked: in plain code, under the schema's name, in a rule or query, in `match`, as an argument of a relation call, and as the schema of a relation's rows.
- A goal that binds variables through a [pattern](https://lionlang.dev/docs.html#logic-patterns) gives what the same goal gives when another goal has bound those variables first, so the answers of a body do not depend on the order of its goals.

### Questions and aggregation

- A rule cannot ask a [question](https://lionlang.dev/docs.html#logic-asking) about a relation that depends on the rule's own head, directly or through other rules. That covers a goal under `not`, a goal used as a value, a `find`, and a relation handed to a function. A question that a rule only builds when it runs, as with `eval`, fails then instead.
- An aggregate runs once its inputs are complete. Aggregation may go through recursion only with the lattice aggregates `aggregate/min`, `aggregate/max`, `aggregate/shortest`, and `aggregate/union`, and only when every relation in the recursive cycle aggregates.
- Every rule for an aggregated relation must aggregate the same columns in the same way. Its facts, and the rows of its rules with plain heads, are candidates its aggregates combine, as a [merge](https://lionlang.dev/docs.html#form-relation) combines them.
- A rule that [invents](https://lionlang.dev/docs.html#form-exists) cannot aggregate. Rules that invent wait until every rule that invents nothing has finished, then every one whose head does not hold invents, all at once, and the other rules run on what was invented, until nothing more is.

Together these make every program stratified: it has a single answer, whatever order rules and facts were added in, unknowns included.

### Termination

- Values flow from the columns a rule's body reads to the columns of its head. A rule may make a new value for a column, by computing it, in the head itself or through `=` or `in`, or by [inventing](https://lionlang.dev/docs.html#form-exists) it, as long as that value never flows back, through the rules, into making another new value. Values that come from facts are not new. So every new value comes from a finite chain of others, and evaluation stops.
- A rule that breaks this fails when it is added. A computed value that flows back fails with `... computes a new value in its head while recursing, which may never finish.`, which suggests computing it in a non-recursive rule or with a lattice aggregate, and an invented one with `... invents a value for "?m" in its head while recursing, which may never finish.`
- Recursion through a lattice aggregate stops when no value improves. If values still improve after 10,000 rounds, as with a negative-weight cycle under `aggregate/min`, the query fails instead of running forever.
- A graph algorithm cannot be part of a recursive cycle.

Here a recursive rule computes a label for each path. No rule reads the label to make another value, so the rule is accepted:

**Example: A computed value that never flows back**

```json
["begin",
  ["relation", "edge", ["from", "to"]],
  ["relation", "path", ["from", "to", "label"]],
  ["fact", ["edge", "a", "b"], ["edge", "b", "c"]],
  ["rule", ["path", "?x", "?y", ["string/concat", "?x", "→", "?y"]], ["edge", "?x", "?y"]],
  ["rule", ["path", "?x", "?z", ["string/concat", "?x", "→", "?z"]], ["path", "?x", "?y", "?_"], ["edge", "?y", "?z"]],
  ["query", ["path", "?from", "?to", "?label"], {"order": ["from", "to"]}]]
```

Result:

```json
[
  {"from":"a","to":"b","label":"a→b"},
  {"from":"a","to":"c","label":"a→c"},
  {"from":"b","to":"c","label":"b→c"}
]
```

Every person has a mother, and every mother is a person. Each mother a rule invents would be a person who needs a mother of her own, so the second rule is refused, and the message names the rule that would invent:

**Example: An invented value that flows back**

```json
["begin",
  ["relation", "person", ["name"]],
  ["relation", "mother", ["child", "mother"]],
  ["rule", ["exists", ["?m"], ["mother", "?p", "?m"]], ["person", "?p"]],
  ["rule", ["person", "?m"], ["mother", "?p", "?m"]]]
```

Error:

```text
LogicError: Rule ["rule",["exists",["?m"],["mother","?p","?m"]],["person","?p"]] invents a value for "?m" in its head while recursing, which may never finish. Invent the value in a rule that does not recurse.
```

### Keys

- A keyed relation holds at most one row per key. A fact with a key that is present replaces the old row.
- Rules can derive rows of a keyed relation, but two different derived rows with the same key make a query that reads them fail, naming both rows and a rule that gives one now. It names the same rows and the same rule whatever order the rules and facts came in, and whether the rows were derived from nothing or followed through changes. The rows are kept, so asking again fails at once, and the next change is followed through them. A relation that merges joins its merged columns instead, and the rest must agree.
- The exception is an [unknown](https://lionlang.dev/docs.html#form-some) that a rule of the keyed relation, or of a relation in a recursive cycle with it, invented. When two rows with the same key differ only where one holds such an unknown, the unknown takes the other row's value, or, when both hold one, the one that nests fewer unknowns, and of those the one that sorts first, and every row that holds it is replaced. So the value kept never depends on the order rules or facts were added in. An unknown that a fact holds is given, so a key never changes it.

Here twins share a mother, and an equality rule makes each child's invented mother the one registered for her. Making Ann and Bea twins would give Ann two mothers, Eve and Fay, which the key cannot make one, so the equality rule refuses the change. The message names Fay as derived, since she sorts later, by the rule that passes a twin's mother on:

**Example: Two mothers a key cannot make one**

```json
["begin",
  ["relation", "person", ["name"]],
  ["relation", "twin", ["a", "b"]],
  ["relation", "registered", ["child", "mother"]],
  ["relation", "mother", ["child", "mother"], {"key": "child"}],
  ["rule", ["exists", ["?m"], ["mother", "?c", "?m"]], ["person", "?c"]],
  ["rule", ["mother", "?a", "?m"], ["twin", "?a", "?b"], ["mother", "?b", "?m"]],
  ["rule", ["=", "?m", "?r"], ["mother", "?c", "?m"], ["registered", "?c", "?r"]],
  ["fact", ["person", "ann"], ["person", "bea"], ["registered", "ann", "eve"], ["registered", "bea", "fay"]],
  ["fact", ["twin", "ann", "bea"]]]
```

Error:

```text
LogicError: "mother" is keyed by ["child"], but ["rule",["mother","?a","?m"],["twin","?a","?b"],["mother","?b","?m"]] derived ["mother","ann","fay"] while ["mother","ann","eve"] holds.
```

### Changes are all or nothing

A form that changes the database, `fact`, `retract`, or `rule`, either makes all of its changes or fails and makes none of them. Every fact is checked before any is added or removed, and every rule before it is added. When the database has [invariants](https://lionlang.dev/docs.html#form-invariant), the form is checked against them after making its changes, and undone if any breaks or cannot be checked, leaving the database exactly as it was, facts in the same order. Separate forms are separate changes.

A change to facts is checked against the invariants that read what it changed, and an invariant that expects no answers is asked about the new rows alone when its goal matches the rows of the relation that changed. That is only a faster way to the same verdict: a change is kept exactly when every invariant still holds.

### Adding what is already held

Adding something the database already holds changes nothing: a fact that is present, a relation or schema declared the same way, or a rule or invariant that a snapshot would write the same way. Rules and invariants hold values as they were evaluated, so a name and the value bound to it are the same, whether the value is data or a function, while a variable `"?x"` and the string `["quote", "?x"]` differ. Running a program twice against one database therefore leaves it as running it once did.

### Equivalent ways to answer

- Goal-directed and full evaluation give the same answers, possibly in a different order. A goal-directed query derives only the rows it asks about, so it does not fail on a row it never derives. A relation that rules invent rows of is derived in full, since what such a rule adds depends on every row. Either way, a relation is derived only when a goal reads it with an answer to extend, so neither fails on a relation that no answer reaches.
- What the database has derived for earlier queries never changes an answer: a query gives what it would give on a database that has derived nothing yet.
- A snapshot, evaluated into an empty database, gives the same answers as the database it was taken from, and taking a snapshot of that gives the same program.
- The relation option `"schema"` and the invariant it stands for keep the same changes, with the same messages, and are saved as the same snapshot.
- What rules derive is kept, and brought up to date when facts or rules change; what is kept is what evaluation from nothing would give.

### Answer order

Without the `"order"` option, a query's answers come in the order they are found. That order is deterministic for a given program and version of Lion, but it is not part of the language: it can differ with what the database had derived before, and with the changes it has seen. Sort with [`"order"`](https://lionlang.dev/docs.html#query-options) when order matters. A `find` always returns its list sorted, so a value a rule derives from one never depends on how it was found.

---

## Errors

URL: https://lionlang.dev/docs.html#errors
Section: Reference (Reference)

> Every way a Lion program can fail, the error's tag, and what causes it.

A failed evaluation is a typed Effect failure. Each error has a `_tag` you can catch with `Effect.catchTag`. On this page and in the editor, failures show as `Tag: message`.

| Tag | Raised when |
| --- | --- |
| `SchemaError` | The program is not a valid Lion expression, such as a record key `__proto__`, or `eval` is given something that is not JSON. |
| `UnboundNameError` | A string of the form `module/name` is evaluated, nothing is bound to it, and it reads as a misspelled name: other names of its module are bound, or a bound name is a letter or two away, which the message suggests. The error holds the string as `unbound` and the suggestion, or `null`, as `nearest`. Inside `quote` the string is data. |
| `InvalidFunctionCallError` | An array's first element does not evaluate to a function, including a string no scope declares. A misspelled `module/name` is an `UnboundNameError` instead. |
| `MalformedFormError` | An array starts with a special form's name that no scope declares, but does not have the form's shape, such as `["define", "x"]`. The message says what the form takes, with an example. The error holds the array as `expression`, the form's name as `form`, and what it takes as `usage`. |
| `UndefinedYetError` | A name is read before the `define`, `relation`, or `schema` form that binds it has run. A body declares the names it defines from its start, so the string means that definition, which has no value yet. A body that defines the name of a form it uses, as `["define", "define", 1]` does, fails with it too, and the message says so. The error holds the name as `unassigned`. |
| `ArithmeticError` | Arithmetic has no result, as division by zero has none, or a whole power would have more than 4,300 digits. Numbers are exact, so no sum or product overflows. A value is written as JSON text with a fraction no decimal writes, such as 1/3, which JSON cannot hold. |
| `LogicError` | A logic form fails: an unsafe goal or rule, a recursion or question that breaks the rules, a broken invariant or query assertion, a key conflict, a bad option, and more. The message says what and where. A function called with the wrong number of arguments, or with an argument it does not take, fails with one too, as `"number/add" takes a number as argument 1 but got "one".` |
| `WaitingError` | A value was needed before it is known. A host function gets this error from [`call`](https://lionlang.dev/docs.html#api-function) when a Lion function's value is not known yet; the call the host function is part of then waits, so a program does not see it. A program sees it when a `fact`, `retract`, or `why` written inside a rule, query, or `find` is given a question: those forms act right away, so they cannot wait. |
| `NotAnObjectError` | A function that reads keys received something that is not an object, or a method function received `null`. |
| `KeyNotFoundError` | `object/get-path` reached a key that is not there. |
| `IndexOutOfBoundsError` | `object/get-path` indexed past the end of a list. |
| `NotAnArrayError` | `object/get-path` used a numeric segment on something that is not a list. |
| `PathTraversalError` | A path passed through a value that is not an object before its last key, or a key that is not there. |
| `InvalidPathError` | A path argument is not a string. |
| `NotAFunctionError` | `object/call-method` or `object/get-method` named something that is not a method. |
| `MethodNotFoundError` | The end of a method path is not a method. |
| `EmptyPathError` | A method path is empty. |
| `NotAConstructorError` | `object/new` was given something that is not a class. |

### Examples

**Example: UnboundNameError**

```json
["number/plus", 1, 2]
```

Error:

```text
UnboundNameError: Nothing is bound to "number/plus". Other names begin with "number/", so it reads as a misspelled name. To mean the string itself, write ["quote", "number/plus"].
```

**Example: InvalidFunctionCallError**

```json
["plus", 1, 2]
```

Error:

```text
InvalidFunctionCallError: ["plus",1,2] is not a valid call. The first element must be a special form or evaluate to a function.
```

**Example: MalformedFormError**

```json
["define", "x"]
```

Error:

```text
MalformedFormError: ["define","x"] is not a well-formed define form: define takes a name and an expression, as in ["define", "answer", 42].
```

**Example: UndefinedYetError**

```json
["begin", ["define", "total", ["number/add", "tax", 1]], ["define", "tax", 2]]
```

Error:

```text
UndefinedYetError: "tax" is read before it is defined. A define binds its name from the start of the body it is in, and a relation or schema form from the start of the program, so the string means that definition, which has no value yet. Define it first, or write ["quote", "tax"] to mean the string.
```

**Example: ArithmeticError**

```json
["number/divide", 1, 0]
```

Error:

```text
ArithmeticError: number/divide: 1 ÷ 0 has no finite result.
```

**Example: A fraction JSON cannot hold**

```json
["number/divide", 1, 3]
```

Error:

```text
ArithmeticError: 1/3 is a fraction no decimal writes, so JSON cannot hold it: round it with ["number/round", value, places], or write it as text with number/toString.
```

**Example: A lambda given one argument too few**

```json
["begin",
  ["define", "pair", ["lambda", ["a", "b"], ["array/make", "a", "b"]]],
  ["pair", 1]]
```

Error:

```text
LogicError: "pair" takes 2 arguments but got 1.
```

**Example: An argument a function does not take**

```json
["number/add", "one", 2]
```

Error:

```text
LogicError: "number/add" takes a number as argument 1 but got "one".
```

**Example: LogicError**

```json
["begin",
  ["relation", "edge", ["from", "to"]],
  ["relation", "lonely", ["node"]],
  ["rule", ["lonely", "?n"], ["not", ["edge", "?n", "?_"]]]]
```

Error:

```text
LogicError: Unsafe rule head ["lonely","?n"]: ?n never appears in a relation in the body. To say the head holds for some value nobody has given, list it in "exists": ["exists", ["?n"], head].
```

**Example: KeyNotFoundError**

```json
["object/get-path", ["quote", {"a": {"b": 1}}], "a.c"]
```

Error:

```text
KeyNotFoundError: There is no key "c" in {"b":1}.
```

### The functions a failure left

A failure that leaves the body of a function says so: its message ends with the functions it left, innermost first. A function has a name there when a `define` bound it, as in Racket. A function that made its call in tail position has nothing left of its own when the failure passes, as in Scheme, so it is not named; neither is a function no `define` bound. The failure keeps its kind.

**Example: A failure names the functions it left**

```json
["begin",
  ["define", "next", ["lambda", ["n"], ["number/add", "n", 1]]],
  ["define", "label", ["lambda", ["n"], ["string/concat", "item ", ["next", "n"]]]],
  ["label", "seven"]]
```

Error:

```text
LogicError: "number/add" takes a number as argument 1 but got "seven". (in "next", called from "label")
```

### Errors inside rules and queries

A function that fails while a rule or query runs it fails the rule or query. A function given a value it does not take says which function, which argument, and what it got, as it does in plain code. Any other failure is a `LogicError` that names the call and the values it ran on. An `ArithmeticError` stays as it is, since it already names both. A filter that is not `true` or `false`, and an answer that is not data, fail with a `LogicError` too.

**Example: A failing filter**

```json
["begin",
  ["relation", "reading", ["value"]],
  ["fact", ["reading", 4], ["reading", "n/a"]],
  ["query", ["and", ["reading", "?v"], ["number/greaterThan", "?v", 3]]]]
```

Error:

```text
LogicError: "number/greaterThan" takes a number as argument 1 but got "n/a".
```

### Errors from host functions

A host function that returns a failed Effect fails the program with that Effect's error. A host function that throws, or a defect inside the evaluator, fails the program as a defect rather than a typed error; `Effect.runPromise` rejects with it.

---

## Command line

URL: https://lionlang.dev/docs.html#cli
Section: Reference (Reference)

> The lion command from @lionlang/cli: evaluating files, keeping a database file, serving the graph editor, and printing Lion as a Web Worker.

Install with `bun add --dev @lionlang/cli`. The package provides the `lion` command.

### `lion [...]`

```shell
lion [--database <path>] [--read-only] [--bind <name=json>]... [--bind-file <name=path>]... [--eval <json>] [<file>...]
```

Reads one or more Lion programs as JSON from `file`s (evaluated sequentially against one database, each with a fresh top-level environment), `--eval` (`-e`), or standard input (when `file` is `-` or omitted while stdin is piped), evaluates them with the standard library and any `--bind` / `--bind-file` bindings, and prints the final result as JSON indented by two spaces.

| Argument or flag | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `file...` | One or more paths to Lion programs in JSON (run in order against one database), or `-` to read from standard input. Optional when `--eval` is passed or stdin is piped. |
| `--eval `, `-e ` | Evaluate a Lion program written directly on the command line instead of reading files. |
| `--bind `, `-b ` | Bind a top-level name to a JSON value, preserving exact decimals and large integers. Repeatable; overrides `--bind-file` for the same name. |
| `--bind-file ` | Bind a top-level name to the JSON value read from a file, preserving exact numbers. Repeatable. |
| `--database ` | A JSON file that holds the logic database. It is loaded before the programs run; if it does not exist, the database starts empty. After all programs succeed, the database is saved back as a [snapshot](https://lionlang.dev/docs.html#form-snapshot) (one form and one fact per line) only if the file did not exist or the database changed. If any program fails, the file is not written. |
| `--read-only`, `-r` | Load `--database` without ever writing changes back to disk, even if the program asserts or retracts facts or rules. |

### `lion inspect []`

```shell
lion inspect [--derived] (<file> | --database <path>)
```

Loads a saved database read-only and prints a concise JSON summary of its ontology: every relation (columns, key, merge, base fact count, rule count, and optionally total derived row count with `--derived`), every named schema and its shape, every invariant, and summary totals.

| Argument or flag | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `file` / `--database ` | Path to the saved Lion database file to inspect. Never modified. |
| `--derived`, `-d` | Also evaluate rules and include total row counts (`rows`) for each relation. |

### `lion check []`

```shell
lion check [--database <path>] [--bind <name=json>]... [--bind-file <name=path>]... [--eval <json>] [<file>]
```

Reads a program without running it and prints a JSON list of diagnostics and warnings, each with its JSON pointer in `at`: malformed forms, misspelled namespaced names, wrong-arity calls to known functions, relations, schemas, or lambdas, invalid `relation`/`query`/`invariant` options, unsafe rule heads or `find` templates, logic variables in ground `fact`s, unreachable or non-exhaustive `match` cases, unreachable `cond` branches after `else`, duplicate lambda parameters, near-miss bare call heads, and Lion lints such as lists written as bare arrays inside rules or queries. Exits with status `1` when any `error` is found.

| Argument or flag | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `file` | Path to a Lion program in JSON, or `-` to read from standard input. Optional when `--eval` is passed or stdin is piped. |
| `--eval `, `-e ` | Check a Lion program written directly on the command line. |
| `--bind `, `-b ` | Declare a top-level binding while checking the program. Repeatable. |
| `--bind-file ` | Declare a top-level binding from a JSON file while checking the program. Repeatable. |
| `--database ` | Load a saved database read-only before checking, so calls to its declared relations and schemas are recognized and checked for arity without modifying the file. |

### `lion repl`

```shell
lion repl [--host <address>] [--port <number>]
```

Serves the Fold Map graph editor bundled with the command, and prints its address. It runs until stopped.

| Flag | Default | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `--host` | `127.0.0.1` | Address to listen on. |
| `--port` | `3000` | Port to listen on, from 1 to 65535. |

### `lion worker`

```shell
lion worker > lion-worker.js
```

Prints the command's own Lion as a Web Worker script, for a page that runs Lion in a browser. The worker holds one logic database. Each message posted to it has an `id`, and each answer it posts back has the same `id`, `ok`, the value as JSON text in `json` or the reason in `error`, and `ms`, how long it took.

| Message | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `{"type": "load", "snapshot": saved}` | Loads a database from a saved one, as `--database` loads its file, in place of the one the worker held. |
| `{"type": "run", "program": program}` | Runs a program against the database, as `lion --database` does. A program can change the database. |

These are the answers the worker gives to a database of edges and the paths they make, and two programs run against it, without `ms`:

```text
{"id":1,"type":"load","snapshot":["begin",
  ["relation","edge",["from","to"]],["relation","path",["from","to"]],
  ["fact",["edge","a","b"],["edge","b","c"]],
  ["rule",["path","?x","?y"],["edge","?x","?y"]],
  ["rule",["path","?x","?z"],["path","?x","?y"],["edge","?y","?z"]]]}
  answers {"id":1,"ok":true,"json":"null"}
{"id":2,"type":"run","program":["find","?to",["path","a","?to"]]}
  answers {"id":2,"ok":true,"json":"[\"b\",\"c\"]"}
{"id":3,"type":"run","program":["path","a"]}
  answers {"id":3,"ok":false,"error":"\"path\" takes 2 arguments (from, to) but got 1."}
```

A page that carries the script runs the Lion of the command that printed it, so running the page's programs with that command checks the page.

### Global flags

| Flag | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `--help`, `-h` | Show help for the command or subcommand. |
| `--version`, `-v` | Show the version. |
| `--wizard` | Build the command interactively. |
| `--completions ` | Print a completion script for `bash`, `zsh`, `fish`, `powershell`, `sh`, or `pwsh`. |
| `--log-level ` | Minimum log level: `all`, `trace`, `debug`, `info`, `warn`, `error`, `fatal`, or `none`. |

### Exit status

`0` when the program succeeds. `1` when the file cannot be read or parsed, the program fails, or the database cannot be loaded or saved; the error is printed.

---

## TypeScript API

URL: https://lionlang.dev/docs.html#typescript-api
Section: Reference (Reference)

> The exports of @lionlang/core and @lionlang/typesafe-ai that host applications use.

Every module of `@lionlang/core` is importable by path, such as `@lionlang/core/evaluation/evaluate`. These are the exports meant for host applications. Evaluation results are Effects; see [Run Lion from TypeScript](https://lionlang.dev/docs.html#run-from-typescript).

### `@lionlang/core/evaluation/evaluate`

#### `run(expression, environment, options?)`

Decodes `expression` as a Lion program and evaluates it with `environment`, a record of bindings. Returns an `Effect` of the result, failing with a [Lion error](https://lionlang.dev/docs.html#errors).

`options.database`: a `LogicDatabase` to use instead of an empty one. Its relations are bound by name, unless `environment` binds the same name.

#### `watch(query, environment, database, onChange)`

Watches a query of a database: `query` is Lion code, such as a `find`, run as `run` runs it against `database`. Returns an `Effect` of `{answers, stop}`: what the query gives now, and a function that stops the watching. After each change a `fact`, `retract`, `rule`, or `invariant` form makes that adds or takes away an answer, `onChange` is called with `{answers, added, removed}`. The database keeps what it derived up to date as facts change, so asking again costs what the change costs. A change an invariant refuses, and what `assuming` asks, tell nothing.

```ts
const database = new LogicDatabase();
await Effect.runPromise(run(setup, stdlib, { database }));
const { answers, stop } = await Effect.runPromise(
  watch(["find", "?to", ["path", "a", "?to"]], stdlib, database, ({ added, removed }) =>
    console.log("reachable now", added, "no longer", removed)
  )
);
await Effect.runPromise(run(["fact", ["edge", "c", "d"]], stdlib, { database }));
// reachable now [ "d" ] no longer []
stop();
```

#### `evaluate(expression)`

Evaluates an already decoded expression. Requires `LionEnvironmentService` and, for logic forms, `LionDatabaseService`. Most hosts use `run`.

### `@lionlang/core/modules`

#### `stdlib`

The [standard library](https://lionlang.dev/docs.html#standard-library) as a record of bindings.

#### `namespaceEntries(namespace, record)`

Returns a copy of `record` with every key prefixed by `namespace/`.

### `@lionlang/core/logic/database`

#### `new LogicDatabase(options?)`

A logic database to share across runs. It holds relations, schemas, facts, rules, and invariants.

`options.goalDirected`: when `false`, every query derives every row of the relations it reads instead of only what it can reach. Defaults to `true`.

### `@lionlang/core/logic/fit`

#### `fits(schema, value)`

An Effect that gives whether a value [fits](https://lionlang.dev/docs.html#schema-fitting) a schema. A host function that takes a schema can check values with it. Like `call`, it needs what an evaluation provides.

#### `problemsOf(schema, value)`

An Effect that gives every place where the value does not fit, as [`schema/problems`](https://lionlang.dev/docs.html#module-schema) does.

#### `misfit(schema, value)`

An Effect that gives the sentence `schema/assert` fails with, or `undefined` when the value fits.

### `@lionlang/core/logic/model`

#### `MAX_LATTICE_ROUNDS`

10,000: the rounds recursion through lattice aggregates may take before failing.

### `@lionlang/core/evaluation/special-forms/function`

#### `call(fn, ...args)`

Calls a Lion function, such as a lambda a host function was given, and returns an `Effect` of its value. A goal the function returns is [asked](https://lionlang.dev/docs.html#logic-asking), so the value is `true` or `false`. If the value is not known yet, the Effect fails with `WaitingError` and the call the host function is part of waits. Use it in a host function that works with what its callback returns.

#### `apply(fn, args)`

Calls a function the way a Lion call does, and returns an `Effect` of what the call evaluates to, which can be a value that waits.

### `@lionlang/core/logic/snapshot`

#### `saveDatabase(database, options?)`

Returns an `Effect` of the database as a snapshot program. Recursive and mutually recursive lambdas are closed into self-contained blocks; fails with `LogicError` only if a rule or invariant holds a function the environment does not name and cannot write.

`options.isBound(name)`: names bound where the snapshot will be loaded; strings equal to them are quoted.

#### `loadDatabase(program, environment)`

Evaluates `program` into a new `LogicDatabase` and returns an `Effect` of it.

### `@lionlang/core/logic/algorithms`

#### `defineAlgorithm({ name, inputs, columns, run })`

Returns a function to bind under `name`. Called in Lion with its inputs and one term per column, it builds a goal over the rows `run` computes.

- `inputs`: a list of `{ kind: "relation" | "value", name }`. A relation input is given as a relation's name or value; a value input as JSON data, or as a logic variable that another goal binds.
- `columns`: the output column names.
- `run(inputs)`: receives each relation input as its list of tuples and each value input as itself. Returns a list of rows, each with one value per column, or a string that explains why it cannot. It runs once for each combination of input values a goal asks about.

### `@lionlang/core/logic/terms`

#### `logicFunction(fn)`

Marks a function that takes logic variables as they are, and returns it. Every other function [waits](https://lionlang.dev/docs.html#logic-waiting) when it is called with a logic variable, so mark a function only when it builds a goal from the variables it is given, as a relation does.

#### `new LogicForm(name, parts)`

A logic form, held the way it is written: `new LogicForm("=", [left, right])` is the goal `["=", left, right]` makes, for a logic function to return. The names are `"not"`, `"and"`, `"or"`, `"="`, `"in"`, `"find"`, and `"schema/fits?"`. A relation call is an `Atom`, of the same module.

#### `builtBy(fn, by, args)`

Records that calling `by` with `args` built `fn`, and returns `fn`. The function is then written as that call, in messages and snapshots, as the functions that `func/partial` and the `schema` module make are.

#### `readsOnlyArguments(bindings)`

Marks the functions among the values of a record as reading nothing but their arguments, as every function of the standard library does. Lion cannot see what any other host function reads, so an [invariant](https://lionlang.dev/docs.html#form-invariant) that calls one is asked in full after every change to facts. Marking a function lets such an invariant be asked only about what a change can have broken.

#### `render(value)`

Converts logic values, such as goals and variables, back into the Lion JSON that produces them.

#### `compareValues(a, b)`

The [value order](https://lionlang.dev/docs.html#value-order) Lion sorts by: negative, zero, or positive.

### `@lionlang/core/analysis/analyze`

#### `analyze(expression, environment?)`

Returns a tree describing each part of a program without evaluating it: its kind, its special form, the role of each child, and what each string means there, read by the [scopes](https://lionlang.dev/docs.html#names-and-scope) a run with `environment` reads it by. A string's `meaning` is a `name` or a `binding`, each with the binding it means or makes (a `parameter`, a `define`, a `relation`, a `schema`, or the `environment`'s, with the pointers of the strings that bind it), a `logic-variable`, `data`, `unbound` where only a name can stand and nothing binds one, as at the head of a call, a `form`'s name, or the `keyword` `else`. A part that fails when it runs, a malformed form or an unbound name, has a `diagnostic`: the message of the error the run fails with. The head of a call has none, since it is looked up where the call runs, and code `eval` ran may have bound it by then. The graph editor is built on it.

```typescript
const program = [
  "begin",
  ["define", "total", 0],
  [["lambda", ["n"], ["array/make", "n", "total", "?x", "done"]], 1],
];
for (const { pointer, value, meaning } of flattenAnalysis(
  analyze(program, stdlib)
)) {
  if (meaning?.kind === "name" || meaning?.kind === "binding") {
    console.log(pointer, value, meaning.kind, meaning.binding.kind);
  } else if (meaning) {
    console.log(pointer, value, meaning.kind);
  }
}
// /0 begin form
// /1/0 define form
// /1/1 total binding define
// /2/0/0 lambda form
// /2/0/1/0 n binding parameter
// /2/0/2/0 array/make name environment
// /2/0/2/1 n name parameter
// /2/0/2/2 total name define
// /2/0/2/3 ?x logic-variable
// /2/0/2/4 done data
```

#### `flattenAnalysis(node)`

The nodes of an analysis tree, in order.

#### `isSpecialFormName(value)`

Whether `value` names a special or logic form.

### `@lionlang/core/errors/evaluation`

`InvalidFunctionCallError`, `LogicError`, and `WaitingError`, the tagged error classes described in [Errors](https://lionlang.dev/docs.html#errors).

### Services

`LionEnvironmentService` (`@lionlang/core/services/evaluation`) and `LionDatabaseService` (`@lionlang/core/services/database`) carry the environment and database through evaluation. `run` provides both. `LionAskerService` (`@lionlang/core/services/asker`) says who answers [questions](https://lionlang.dev/docs.html#logic-asking) at the moment: evaluation sets it while a rule is being written and while one runs.

### `@lionlang/typesafe-ai`

#### `makeTypeSafeBindings(config?, namespace?)`

Returns bindings to spread into an environment: `noul`, `choice`, `score`, `system-one`, and `models`, under `namespace/`, `"typesafe"` by default. `config` is the TypeSafe client configuration. See [Ask AI models with TypeSafe](https://lionlang.dev/docs.html#ask-ai-models).

#### `makeTypeSafeModule(config?)`

The same functions without a namespace.

---

## Why programs are JSON

URL: https://lionlang.dev/docs.html#why-json
Section: Explanation (Explanation)

> What Lion gains by making every program a JSON value, what it costs, and how the evaluation rules make it work.

Most languages have a syntax of their own, and a parser that turns text into a tree the evaluator walks. Lion skips the syntax. A Lion program is already the tree, written as JSON, and the evaluator walks it directly. This page explains why that is worth doing, and what it costs.

### Code that other systems can handle

JSON is the one data format almost every system already speaks. Databases store it, HTTP carries it, queues pass it along, and every language can read and write it without a new library. When programs are JSON, all of that infrastructure works on programs too. A rule can live in a database row and be edited by an admin screen. A workflow can arrive in a request body. A diff of a program is a diff of JSON.

It also matters for programs that write programs. A language model, a form builder, or another service can produce a Lion program by producing JSON, and a JSON schema can describe what it may produce. There is no grammar to get wrong and no string escaping to forget.

### Code is data, so data can become code

Lisp's old idea is that code and data share one shape, so a program can build and inspect programs with the same tools it uses on any list. Lion inherits this, which is why it is called a Lisp. A program is a list; [`quote`](https://lionlang.dev/docs.html#form-quote) holds one without running it, list functions take it apart and put it together, and [`eval`](https://lionlang.dev/docs.html#form-eval) runs the result. The [how-to guide on code as data](https://lionlang.dev/docs.html#code-as-data) shows this in practice, and the graph editor relies on it: it edits the JSON tree and nothing else.

### How JSON becomes code
